D.name: Marcos v. Manglapus
D.hook: Leftover power keeps the peace.
D.rule: The President has residual (leftover) powers beyond those listed, and may stop a citizen's return when national security requires it, as long as there is a factual basis.
mem: “The executive power shall be vested in the President of the Philippines.” — Art. VII, Sec. 1
doc: Executive power is **more than the sum** of the listed powers. The President has **residual powers** to protect the general welfare.
The **right to return** is different from the right to travel. It may give way to national security.
**TEST:** Courts only check for **grave abuse of discretion** — was there a factual basis?

**Limit:** residual power cannot override a power the Constitution gives another branch (e.g. Congress’s inquiry in aid of legislation). Bar-style tie-in: E.O. 111 (prior approval before officials appear). [Outside the 28 cases: Senate v. Ermita; verify.]
D.drill: Ramon, a former President ousted years ago and now living in exile abroad, announces that he and about 300 supporters will fly home on the 15th. Military intelligence reports that armed groups loyal to him plan to seize two camps and the main airport once he lands. The President, citing the duty to protect the nation, issues a directive barring his return “until the threat ends.” No law gives the President the power to ban a citizen from coming home. Ramon petitions the Supreme Court. He argues that (a) the Constitution lists no power to bar a citizen from returning, and (b) his right to travel can be impaired only as the Constitution and the law allow. Should the petition be granted? Explain.
alac: No. The petition should not be granted. The directive barring Ramon's return is valid.

The Constitution vests the executive power in the President. Jurisprudence provides that this power is more than the sum of the listed powers; the President has residual powers to protect the general welfare, including keeping peace and order. The right to return is different from the right to travel and may give way to national security. Courts review the President's act only for grave abuse of discretion, that is, whether there was a factual basis.

On (a), the lack of an express power is not decisive, because residual power covers the ban. On (b), Ramon invokes the right to travel, but what he asserts is the right to return, which may be limited for national security. There is a factual basis: intelligence shows armed loyalists plan to seize camps and the airport. The directive is also temporary (“until the threat ends”). There is no grave abuse.
Therefore, the petition should be denied. The directive is valid.
D.key: Do not answer “no power because it is not listed.” Residual power is the answer, but it still needs a factual basis and must be limited to the threat.

D.name: Risos-Vidal v. COMELEC and Lim
D.hook: “Whereas” is not a condition.
D.rule: Pardon power is plenary; a pardon restoring "civil and political rights" lets the person run, and a "whereas" clause is not a condition.
mem: “…the President may grant reprieves, commutations, and pardons, and remit fines and forfeitures, after conviction by final judgment.” — Art. VII, Sec. 19
“No pardon… for violation of election laws… shall be granted by the President without the favorable recommendation of the Commission.” — Art. IX-C, Sec. 5
doc: The pardoning power is **plenary**. Congress cannot add limits by law.
A condition binds only if it is in the **operative (dispositive) part**, not in a "whereas" clause.
D.drill: Dante, a former mayor, was convicted of plunder by final judgment and sentenced to reclusion perpetua with perpetual absolute disqualification. After he served a few years, the President granted him an “absolute pardon.” The pardon papers began with a “WHEREAS” clause stating that Dante had vowed never again to seek public office. The operative part said: “he is hereby restored to his civil and political rights.” Dante files a certificate of candidacy for governor. Rival Elena petitions to disqualify him. She argues that (a) the “whereas” clause is a condition that bars him from running, and (b) a law Congress passed last year forbids pardons for plunder convicts until they have served twenty years. Should Elena's petition be granted? Explain.
alac: No. Elena's petition should not be granted. Dante may run.

The Constitution gives the President the power to grant pardons after conviction by final judgment. Jurisprudence provides that the pardoning power is plenary and cannot be limited by Congress by law. A pardon that expressly restores civil and political rights lifts the perpetual disqualification, and a condition binds only if it is in the operative part, not in a “whereas” clause.

On (a), the vow not to seek office appears only in the “whereas” clause, so it is not a condition. The operative part expressly restores Dante's political rights, so his disqualification is lifted. On (b), Congress cannot add a twenty-year wait because that would limit a plenary constitutional power. Dante's conviction was by final judgment, so the pardon was proper.
Therefore, Elena's petition should be denied. Dante may run for governor.
D.key: Two checks: (1) Is the limit in the operative part? A “whereas” clause is not a condition. (2) Is Congress trying to limit the pardon? It cannot. A pardon needs a final judgment first.

D.name: Trillanes v. Medialdea
D.hook: Two keys lock it. One key can't open it.
D.rule: Amnesty needs the President plus a majority of all Members of Congress, so the President alone cannot revoke it; revoking it without a hearing also violates due process.
mem: “He shall also have the power to grant amnesty with the concurrence of a majority of all the Members of the Congress.” — Art. VII, Sec. 19
doc: Amnesty is a **joint act** of the President and Congress. The President **cannot revoke it alone**.
Revoking a granted amnesty without notice and hearing violates **due process**.
Delegating the **processing** of applications to the DND is valid (not undue delegation).
D.drill: Lt. Santos and 300 soldiers took part in a failed mutiny years ago. A later President granted them amnesty by proclamation, which a majority of all Members of Congress concurred in. A committee of the Department of National Defense (DND) processed their applications. Years later, a new President issues a proclamation declaring Santos' amnesty “void ab initio” because he allegedly never filed an application or admitted guilt. The proclamation orders the reopening of the criminal case and Santos' arrest, with no notice or hearing. Santos goes to court. He argues that (a) the President alone cannot revoke the amnesty, (b) his amnesty was revoked without due process, and (c) the proclamation is invalid because the DND, not Congress, processed the applications. Should Santos' petition be granted? Explain.
alac: Partly. Santos is correct on (a) and (b), but wrong on (c). The petition should be granted.

The Constitution requires the concurrence of a majority of all Members of Congress for amnesty. Jurisprudence provides that amnesty is a joint act of the President and Congress, so the President cannot revoke it alone. Revoking a granted amnesty without notice and hearing violates due process. Delegating the processing of applications to the DND is valid because it is not undue delegation.

On (a), the grant needed Congress, so the new President alone cannot undo it by proclamation. On (b), Santos was arrested and his case reopened with no notice or hearing, which violates due process. On (c), the DND only processed applications and did not decide the amnesty itself, so there was no undue delegation.
Therefore, the proclamation is invalid as to Santos. The petition should be granted, but the argument on delegation fails.
D.key: Amnesty is a joint act; revoking it needs the same joint act and a hearing. But do not call delegation of mere processing to an agency invalid.

D.name: Pangilinan v. Cayetano
D.hook: The exit door has two locks.
D.rule: The President may withdraw from a treaty, except when the Senate made its concurrence depend on its consent to withdrawal, or when a later law implements the treaty.
mem: “No treaty or international agreement shall be valid and effective unless concurred in by at least two-thirds of all the Members of the Senate.” — Art. VII, Sec. 21
doc: The President, as primary architect of foreign policy, may withdraw — but this power is **not absolute**.
The President **may** withdraw from a treaty obviously contrary to the Constitution or a statute.
Senators suing individually lack standing if the **Senate as a body** passed no resolution.
D.drill: The Philippines joined an international convention by treaty. The Senate concurred in a resolution that said nothing on withdrawal. Later, the President notified the other parties that the Philippines is withdrawing from the convention, without asking the Senate. Four senators sue in their personal capacity to nullify the withdrawal. They argue that (a) a treaty made with Senate concurrence cannot be withdrawn without the Senate, and (b) in any case the withdrawal violates a law Congress passed years later that implements the convention. The Senate as a body passed no resolution on the matter. Should the petition be granted? Explain.
alac: No. The petition should not be granted. The senators lack standing, and, in any case, the withdrawal is valid.

The President is the primary architect of foreign policy and may withdraw from a treaty. Jurisprudence provides that this power is not absolute: it cannot be used when the Senate made its concurrence depend on its consent to withdrawal, or when a later law implements the treaty. Senators suing individually lack standing if the Senate as a body passed no resolution.

On standing, the four senators sue alone, and the Senate as a body passed no resolution, so they have no standing. On (a), the Senate resolution said nothing about withdrawal, so no condition was attached. On (b), the later implementing law is a real limit if it makes the treaty part of domestic law. If the law does implement the convention, the President cannot undo it by withdrawal alone, because that would amount to repealing a statute.
Therefore, the petition should be dismissed for lack of standing. If it were heard, (a) fails, but (b) succeeds if the later law truly implements the convention.
D.key: Standing first (individual senators have none without a Senate resolution). Then check two exceptions to the President's power to withdraw: Senate conditions on withdrawal, and a later implementing law.

D.name: Colmenares v. Duterte
D.hook: Can't sue the President. Loan needs the Monetary Board.
D.rule: A sitting President cannot be sued in any case; foreign loans need the Monetary Board's concurrence; information on foreign loans must be made public.
mem: “The President may contract or guarantee foreign loans… with the prior concurrence of the Monetary Board.” — Art. VII, Sec. 20
“Information on foreign loans obtained or guaranteed by the Government shall be made available to the public.” — Art. XII, Sec. 21
doc: **Presidential immunity:** a sitting President cannot be sued, whatever the case. Drop the President; the case continues against the other officials.
Loans are valid if made with **Monetary Board concurrence**.
**Confidentiality clauses** cannot defeat the right to information on foreign loans.
D.drill: Advocacy groups sue the sitting President, the Finance Secretary, and the Monetary Board for approving a foreign loan. They ask the court to (a) declare the loan invalid, (b) order the release of the loan agreements, and (c) hold the President liable for the loan. The government replies that (i) the President cannot be sued, (ii) the Monetary Board concurred in the loan, so it is valid, and (iii) the loan agreements contain a confidentiality clause that bars their release. Rule on the contentions. Explain.
alac: The government is right on (i) and (ii), but wrong on (iii).

Jurisprudence provides that a sitting President cannot be sued in any case, whatever the case. The President is dropped, and the case continues against the other officials. Foreign loans are valid if made with the concurrence of the Monetary Board. A confidentiality clause cannot defeat the people's right to information on foreign loans.

On (i), the President is immune, so the suit is dismissed as to the President only. The case continues against the Finance Secretary and the Monetary Board. On (ii), the Monetary Board concurred, so the loan is not invalid on that ground. On (iii), the right to information on foreign loans is constitutional, and a private clause cannot override it.
Therefore, the case is dropped against the President, the loan stands, and the government must disclose the loan agreements.
D.key: Three separate answers: immunity (drop the President only), validity (Monetary Board concurrence), disclosure (confidentiality clause cannot defeat the right to information).

D.name: Velicaria-Garafil v. Office of the President
D.hook: Appointment is a four-step dance. Finish before the music stops.
D.rule: Appointment is a process; all four steps must be finished before the two-month election ban starts.
mem: “Two months immediately before the next presidential elections and up to the end of his term, a President or Acting President shall not make appointments, except temporary appointments to executive positions when continued vacancies therein will prejudice public service or endanger public safety.” — Art. VII, Sec. 15
D.drill: The presidential election is on May 9. The two-month ban on appointments by the President starts on March 9 and runs to the end of the term. The outgoing President signs 25 appointment papers on March 4. The papers are sent to the Office of the President's records section on March 8, but the appointees physically receive their papers on March 10. Eight of them take their oaths on March 11. The incoming President recalls the appointments and calls them void for violating the ban. The appointees argue that the President signed the papers before the ban. Are the appointments valid? Explain.
alac: No. The appointments are void because they were not completed before the ban started.

Jurisprudence provides that appointment is a process with four steps: (1) the authority to appoint and its exercise, shown by signing; (2) transmittal of the appointment paper; (3) receipt by the appointee; and (4) acceptance, shown by oath and assumption. All four must be completed before the two-month ban begins. The only exception is a temporary appointment where continued vacancies would prejudice public service or endanger public safety.

Here, the President signed on March 4, but the appointees received the papers on March 10 and took their oath on March 11, all after the ban started on March 9. Signing alone is not enough. No facts show that the posts were needed to prevent harm to public service or public safety, so the exception does not apply.
Therefore, the appointments are void.
D.key: Signing is only step 1 of 4. Count all four steps against the ban date. Without a showing of public-service necessity, the exception fails.

D.name: De Castro v. JBC
D.hook: The ban is for the Executive, not the judges.
D.rule: The appointments ban covers only the Executive Department, so the President may fill Judiciary vacancies (even Chief Justice) during the ban.
mem: “Any vacancy shall be filled within ninety days from the occurrence thereof.” — Art. VIII, Sec. 4(1)
doc: Sec. 15 is in **Article VII** (Executive). The framers did not put it in Article VIII.
Art. VIII, Sec. 4(1) says "shall" — the **90-day period is mandatory**.
The **JBC process** already prevents the abuses the ban targets.
*In re Valenzuela* (1998) was **reversed**.
D.drill: The Chief Justice will retire on May 15. The presidential election is on May 9, and the ban on appointments begins March 9. The outgoing President says the Judicial and Bar Council (JBC) must send its shortlist so that a successor can be appointed in time. A lawyers' group sues. It argues that (a) the ban applies to the Judiciary, so the President cannot appoint a Chief Justice during the ban, and (b) the 90-day period in the Constitution to fill Supreme Court vacancies should be suspended. Should the petition be granted? Explain.
alac: No. The petition should not be granted. The President may appoint the Chief Justice during the ban.

Jurisprudence provides that the ban on appointments is found in the article on the Executive Department and does not cover the Judiciary. The article on the Judiciary says vacancies in the Supreme Court “shall” be filled within 90 days, so the period is mandatory. The JBC process already prevents the abuses that the ban is meant to stop. The earlier contrary ruling was reversed.

On (a), the ban is in Article VII, so it does not reach appointments to the Supreme Court. The JBC nominates the candidates, so the President cannot use the appointment for election purposes. On (b), the 90-day period is mandatory and cannot be set aside. The vacancy must be filled within that time.
Therefore, the petition should be denied. The President may appoint the Chief Justice during the ban.
D.key: The ban is in Art. VII and does not touch the Judiciary. The 90-day rule is mandatory (“shall”). Valenzuela was reversed.

D.name: Belgica v. Executive Secretary
D.hook: After the budget passes, hands off.
D.rule: Legislators cannot control funds after the budget is passed; and "such other purposes as the President may direct" is undue delegation.
mem: “No money shall be paid out of the Treasury except in pursuance of an appropriation made by law.” — Art. VI, Sec. 29(1)
“The President shall have the power to veto any particular item or items in an appropriation… bill.” — Art. VI, Sec. 27(2)
doc: **Item** = specific amount for a specific purpose ("singular correspondence").
**Delegation tests:** completeness test + sufficient standard test.

**Bar-style tie-in:** a law letting legislators pick projects and beneficiaries after enactment is post-enactment control (unconstitutional); kickback facts show the harm but are not the legal ground.
D.drill: Following insistent requests from high-ranking DPWH officials, Congress enacts an appropriation law with provisions that let individual legislators decide, after the law is enacted, how much of the funds go to specific flood control projects and which beneficiaries get them. The Department of Budget and Management (DBM) releases funds based on the legislators' lists. In the Senate Blue Ribbon investigation, DPWH officials and contractors testify that most contracts went to contractors owned by or endorsed by legislators' relatives, and that billions in kickbacks were paid to legislators who “inserted” the funds for projects that turned out to be ghost, unfinished, or substandard. A taxpayer petitions the Supreme Court to declare the law unconstitutional. Is the appropriation law unconstitutional? Explain.
alac: Yes. The provisions letting legislators decide post-enactment how funds are spent are unconstitutional.

The Constitution requires that no money be paid from the Treasury except under an appropriation made by law, and gives the President the power to veto items. Jurisprudence provides that an item is a specific amount for a specific purpose. Legislators cannot control funds after the budget is passed, because that is the job of the executive. Delegation is valid only if it passes the completeness test and the sufficient standard test.

Here, the law lets legislators decide after enactment how much goes to which project and beneficiary. This gives legislators a role in executing the law after it has been passed, which belongs to the Executive. It also takes away the President's chance to veto the items, because the specific items are not in the law when it is passed. The law has no standard for the legislators' choices, so it is also an invalid delegation. The kickback testimony only shows the harm of this setup; the defect is in the structure.
Therefore, the provisions are unconstitutional. The disbursements made under them have no valid basis.
D.key: Two defects: (1) post-enactment legislative control of funds violates separation of powers and the veto power; (2) no sufficient standard. Corruption facts show the danger but are not the legal ground.

D.name: Republic v. Sereno
D.hook: Not qualified from the start → quo warranto. Bad acts in office → impeachment.
D.rule: Quo warranto (filed in the Supreme Court) can oust an impeachable officer who was not eligible when appointed; the one-year limit does not bind the State.
mem: “A Member of the Judiciary must be a person of proven competence, integrity, probity, and independence.” — Art. VIII, Sec. 7(3)
“…may be removed from office on impeachment…” — Art. XI, Sec. 2
doc: "**May**" in Art. XI, Sec. 2 is permissive — impeachment is not the only way.
One-year prescription does **not** run against the State.
Failure to file SALNs = lack of proven **integrity**.
D.drill: Atty. Dulce was appointed Justice of the Supreme Court years ago. During her JBC application, she did not submit most of her required Statements of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth (SALNs) and told the JBC that they were “not on file.” A taxpayer later learns that the SALNs were never filed. The Solicitor General files a quo warranto petition in the Supreme Court to oust her. Dulce argues that (a) as an impeachable officer she can be removed only by impeachment, and (b) the petition was filed beyond the one-year period for quo warranto. Should the petition be granted? Explain.
alac: Yes. The petition for quo warranto should be granted.

Jurisprudence provides that the word “may” in Under the Constitution, is permissive, so impeachment is not the only way to remove an impeachable officer who was not eligible to hold office. The one-year prescriptive period does not run against the State. Failure to file SALNs shows a lack of proven integrity, which is a qualification for Members of the Judiciary.

On (a), the question is not removal for a wrong done in office, but whether Dulce was qualified to be appointed in the first place; quo warranto may be used. On (b), the one-year period does not bind the State. On the merits, she did not file the SALNs and said they were not on file. This shows a lack of the integrity the Constitution requires.
Therefore, the petition should be granted. Her appointment is void.
D.key: Impeachment is for wrongs in office; quo warranto tests whether the person was eligible at the start. The one-year limit does not bind the State.

D.name: Jardeleza v. Sereno
D.hook: Strategy is not integrity. A charge must be heard.
D.rule: When the JBC questions an applicant's integrity, it must give notice and a hearing; a disagreement about legal strategy is not an integrity issue.
mem: “A Judicial and Bar Council is hereby created under the supervision of the Supreme Court…” — Art. VIII, Sec. 8(1)
doc: JBC proceedings are *sui generis*, but **due process applies** when integrity is challenged.
The unanimity rule applies only to **integrity** questions, not legal strategy.
The SC corrects the JBC through its **supervision** and its power over grave abuse.
D.drill: Solicitor General Rey is nominated by the JBC for appointment as Associate Justice. At a JBC meeting, a Justice says Rey's integrity is in question for his handling of a sensitive case and, without giving Rey a copy of the charges, asks the Council to exclude him. Rey is called in and told to explain, but he is not told what the objection is. The JBC votes to exclude Rey from the shortlist because one member opposes him. Rey petitions the Supreme Court. He argues that (a) he was denied due process and (b) the JBC's unanimity rule for integrity questions was misapplied because the real issue was a disagreement over his legal strategy. Should the petition be granted? Explain.
alac: Yes. The petition should be granted.

Jurisprudence provides that JBC proceedings are sui generis, but due process applies when the integrity of an applicant is challenged: the applicant is entitled to notice of the charges and an opportunity to be heard. The unanimity rule applies only to integrity questions, not to disagreement over legal strategy. The Supreme Court may correct the JBC through its supervision and its power over grave abuse.

On (a), the objection to Rey's integrity was raised without telling him what it was, so he had no real chance to answer. This violates due process. On (b), a disagreement over legal strategy is not an integrity issue. A single objection should not bar him by invoking unanimity when the real issue is strategy.
Therefore, the petition should be granted. Rey must be given notice of the charge and a chance to be heard, and the JBC should not have excluded him by a single objection on strategy.
D.key: Integrity challenge → notice + hearing. Legal strategy disagreement → not an integrity issue, so no unanimity rule.

D.name: Villanueva v. JBC
D.hook: JBC may add rules — but must publish them.
D.rule: The JBC may add reasonable standards beyond the minimum qualifications, but it must publish them.
mem: “The Council shall have the principal function of recommending appointees to the Judiciary.” — Art. VIII, Sec. 8(5)
doc: The JBC may set **additional standards** to measure "proven competence."
The 5-year rule for first-level judges is a **reasonable classification** (experience) — no equal protection violation.
Applicants have **no vested right** to be nominated.
Policies must be **published**.
D.drill: The JBC announces new policies: (1) only incumbents with at least five years of service as first-level court judges may be nominated to second-level courts, and (2) applicants with pending administrative cases are not considered. These policies were not published in a newspaper. Judge Ana, who has served three years as a first-level judge, applies to an RTC post and is excluded from consideration. Judge Ana petitions the Supreme Court. She argues that (a) the JBC cannot add qualifications beyond those in the Constitution, (b) the five-year rule violates equal protection, and (c) the JBC should have published the policies. Should the petition be granted? Explain.
alac: Partly. The JBC may add the five-year rule, but the policy is not effective against Ana until it is published. The petition should be granted on (c) only.

Jurisprudence provides that the JBC may set additional standards to measure “proven competence” beyond the minimum constitutional qualifications. The five-year rule is a reasonable classification based on experience, so there is no equal protection violation. Applicants have no vested right to be nominated. The JBC's policies must be published.

On (a), the five-year rule is a standard for measuring competence, not a new qualification. On (b), requiring experience is a valid ground for a classification, so Ana is not denied equal protection. On (c), a policy that affects applicants must be published before it can be enforced against them. These policies were not published.
Therefore, the JBC's standards are valid, but they cannot be applied to Ana until published.
D.key: Valid standards + no vested right, but unpublished policies cannot be enforced against applicants.

D.name: Chavez v. JBC
D.hook: "A" representative means ONE.
D.rule: Only one representative of Congress sits in the seven-member JBC; past JBC acts remain valid (operative fact).
mem: “…the Chief Justice as ex officio Chairman, the Secretary of Justice, and a representative of the Congress as ex officio Members, a representative of the Integrated Bar, a professor of law, a retired Member of the Supreme Court, and a representative of the private sector.” — Art. VIII, Sec. 8(1)
doc: **Plain meaning** (verba legis): "a representative" = one.
Seven members is deliberate — an odd number avoids deadlock.
**Operative fact doctrine:** past acts stay valid.
D.drill: Years ago, the JBC allowed both the Senate and the House of Representatives to be represented in the JBC, each with one vote, so the JBC effectively had eight members. During that time, the JBC sent shortlists on which the President based several appointments. A citizen sues now, arguing that (a) the Constitution allows only one representative of Congress in the seven-member JBC, and (b) the nominations and appointments made under the eight-member JBC are void. Should the petition be granted? Explain.
alac: Partly. The petition should be granted on (a), but denied on (b).

Jurisprudence provides that the Constitution says “a representative of Congress,” and under plain meaning (verba legis), that means one. The seven-member size is deliberate, because an odd number avoids deadlock. Under the operative fact doctrine, acts done before the declaration of unconstitutionality remain valid.

On (a), the JBC had two Congress representatives with one vote each, which is contrary to the text. On (b), the JBC's nominations and the President's appointments were made under a law that was in effect and relied on in good faith. The operative fact doctrine protects them.
Therefore, only one representative of Congress sits in the JBC. Past nominations and appointments remain valid.
D.key: Plain meaning: “a representative” = one. Operative fact doctrine protects past acts.

D.name: Aguinaldo v. Aquino
D.hook: No clusters. The President picks from the whole basket.
D.rule: For vacancies that exist at the same time, the JBC cannot cluster nominees; the President may choose from all nominees.
mem: “…shall be appointed by the President from a list of at least three nominees prepared by the Judicial and Bar Council for every vacancy.” — Art. VIII, Sec. 9
doc: **Clustering** limits the President's choice — it encroaches on the appointing power.
"Three per vacancy" is met if the combined list has at least 3 × the number of vacancies.
Seniority follows the **order of appointment**.
D.drill: Five vacancies in the Sandiganbayan exist at the same time. The JBC sends the President a list of 15 nominees but divides them into five clusters of three, one cluster per vacancy. The President wants to choose from all 15 nominees and appoints two from one cluster and three from another. Concerned citizens argue that (a) the President violated the clusters, and (b) the order of appointment should not determine seniority. Is the President correct on (a) and (b)? Explain.
alac: The President is correct on (a). On (b), seniority follows the order of appointment, so the citizens are wrong.

Jurisprudence provides that for vacancies that exist at the same time the JBC cannot cluster nominees. Clustering limits the President's choice and encroaches on the appointing power. The requirement of three nominees per vacancy is met if the combined list has at least three times the number of vacancies. Seniority follows the order of appointment.

On (a), there are five vacancies and 15 nominees, which meets the rule. Clustering is not allowed, so the President may choose from all the 15. On (b), seniority follows the order in which the appointments are made, so the citizens' argument that it should not depend on the order of appointment fails.
Therefore, the clusters did not bind the President. Seniority follows the order of appointment.
D.key: No clustering for simultaneous vacancies. 3 × vacancies is enough. Seniority = order of appointment.

D.name: Re: COA Opinion on Appraised Value of SC Properties
D.hook: The Court sells its own things its own way.
D.rule: COA may audit the Judiciary, but it cannot force its own valuation formula on how the Court disposes of its own property.
mem: “The Judiciary shall enjoy fiscal autonomy.” — Art. VIII, Sec. 3
doc: **Fiscal autonomy** = full flexibility to allocate and use resources, including disposing of property under the Court's own guidelines.
COA still **audits** — it just cannot dictate the Court's valuation.
D.drill: The Supreme Court sells some of its old equipment and houses and decides, under its own guidelines, to let retiring justices buy their service vehicles at a value computed by the Court's formula. The Commission on Audit (COA) audits the sale and says the Court must use COA's formula and must obtain COA's approval. The Court's Office of the Court Administrator refuses, citing fiscal autonomy. The COA says that it audits everyone. Who is correct? Explain.
alac: The Court is correct on the valuation. COA is correct that it may audit.

Fiscal autonomy of the Judiciary means full flexibility to allocate and use its resources, including disposing of property under the Court's own guidelines. Jurisprudence provides that COA may still audit the Judiciary, but it cannot force its own valuation formula on how the Court disposes of its own property.

Here, the Court follows its own guidelines on valuation and sale, which is part of its fiscal autonomy. COA may audit to check that the funds and property were used properly, but it cannot dictate the formula or require its approval.
Therefore, COA may audit the sale but cannot impose its formula on the Court.
D.key: Audit yes, dictate no. Fiscal autonomy protects how the Court handles its own property.

D.name: In re: Judicial Independence v. Abolition of JDF
D.hook: A bill is not a law. No case yet.
D.rule: Courts cannot review a proposed bill because there is no actual case yet.
mem: “Appropriations for the Judiciary may not be reduced by the legislature below the amount appropriated for the previous year and, after approval, shall be automatically and regularly released.” — Art. VIII, Sec. 3
doc: Mandamus cannot compel the Court to act against Congress on its own autonomy.
The JDF comes from **legal fees**, not national appropriations.

**Bar-style tie-in:** a bill lowering the burden of proof is not reviewable until it is law and applied; once applied, the presumption of innocence (proof beyond reasonable doubt) applies. [Art. III, Sec. 14(2) is outside the 28 cases; verify.]
D.drill: As public discussion grows on how to create a more effective justice system to prevent further flood control scandals, a bill is filed in Congress to lower, for crimes involving infrastructure corruption, the burden of proof from proof beyond reasonable doubt to preponderance of evidence. A group of lawyers petitions the Supreme Court to stop Congress from passing the bill and to rule on its validity. Another group asks the Court to rule on the same standard of proof in a rule amendment. Should the Court rule on the proposed bill? Explain.
alac: No. The Court should not rule on the bill now. The petition is premature.

Judicial power requires an actual case or controversy. Jurisprudence provides that courts cannot review a proposed bill because there is no actual case yet. Mandamus cannot compel the Court to act against Congress on its own autonomy.

Here, the bill has not been passed, and no one has been convicted or prosecuted under a lower standard. There is no actual case, only a proposal. The Court cannot rule on a bill that may never become law.
Therefore, the petition should be dismissed. If the bill becomes law and is applied to a case, the question may then be raised.
D.key: No actual case = no judicial review. A bill is not law yet.

D.name: OCA / Flores-Concepcion v. Judge Castañeda
D.hook: Retire: the case lives. Die: the case dies.
D.rule: Retirement or resignation does not end an administrative case filed while in office; death generally does.
mem: “The Supreme Court shall have administrative supervision over all courts and the personnel thereof.” — Art. VIII, Sec. 6
doc: **Rule:** Jurisdiction attaches when the complaint is filed while the respondent is in office; leaving office does not end it.
**Bar-style tie-in:** Congress cannot cite judges in contempt for how they rule; discipline of judges belongs to the Supreme Court. [Outside the 28 cases; verify.]
D.drill: Judge Castañeda is charged with gross misconduct in an administrative complaint filed while he was in office. While the case is pending, he retires. Separately, the complainant asks the Court to drop the case because Judge Castañeda is no longer in office. The Court Administrator argues that the case should continue. In a related matter, the House of Representatives, unhappy with a Court of Appeals decision granting a writ of habeas corpus to officials it cited in contempt, orders the three CA Justices to explain why they should not be cited in contempt. Rule on (a) the retirement and (b) the House's show-cause order. Explain.
alac: On (a), the case should continue. On (b), the House may not cite the Justices in contempt.

Jurisprudence provides that jurisdiction attaches when the complaint is filed while the respondent is in office. Retirement or resignation does not end it. Death generally does. [Beyond the 28 cases: for (b), check this against your own notes.] The Constitution vests the Supreme Court with administrative supervision over all courts and their personnel, and judges may be disciplined or removed only by the Supreme Court. Congress's contempt power is incidental to its power of inquiry in aid of legislation.

On (a), the complaint was filed while the judge was in office, so the Court keeps jurisdiction after his retirement. On (b), the CA Justices were deciding a case. The House is not conducting an inquiry in aid of legislation on them, and it cannot discipline judges, which the Constitution gives to the Supreme Court. Citing them in contempt for a decision would also interfere with judicial independence and with the separation of powers.
Therefore, the case against Judge Castañeda continues. The House cannot cite the Justices in contempt for their decision.
D.key: Jurisdiction attaches at filing, so retirement does not erase the case. Judges answer to the Supreme Court, not to Congress, for how they decide cases.

D.name: Caronan v. Caronan
D.hook: Fake identity → no lawyer.
D.rule: The practice of law is a privilege; admission obtained by fraud is void.
mem: “Promulgate rules concerning… admission to the practice of law…” — Art. VIII, Sec. 5(5)
doc: Law practice is a **privilege**, not a right.
Education and **moral fitness** must exist at admission and **continue**.
Years of honest practice do not cure fraudulent admission.
D.drill: Atty. Lito was admitted to the Bar 15 years ago and has practiced honestly since then. Recently, it is discovered that the person who actually took the bar exams in his name was someone else, and that he never finished his required education. Lito argues that (a) the long years of honest practice cure the defect, and (b) he is already in good standing, so the Court has no power to remove him. Should he be allowed to continue practicing? Explain.
alac: No. Lito should not be allowed to continue practicing. His admission is void.

Jurisprudence provides that the practice of law is a privilege, not a right. Education and moral fitness must exist at admission and continue. Admission obtained by fraud is void, and years of honest practice do not cure it.

On (a), Lito never really passed the exam and never completed his education, so his admission was obtained by fraud. The long period of honest practice does not cure this. On (b), his good standing is based on a void admission. The Supreme Court, which controls admission to the bar, may remove one who was never validly admitted.
Therefore, his admission is void and his name should be removed from the Roll of Attorneys.
D.key: Privilege, not right. Fraud at the start cannot be cured by time.

D.name: Brillantes v. Yorac
D.hook: No acting chair from the Palace.
D.rule: The President cannot designate an acting chairman of a Constitutional Commission, even temporarily.
mem: “The Constitutional Commissions, which shall be independent, are the Civil Service Commission, the Commission on Elections, and the Commission on Audit.” — Art. IX-A, Sec. 1
“In no case shall any Member be appointed or designated in a temporary or acting capacity.” — Art. IX-C, Sec. 1(2) / IX-B / IX-D
doc: A designation revocable at will makes the officer **depend on the President** — this kills independence.
A temporary arrangement is for the **Commission itself** to decide.
D.drill: The Chairman of the Commission on Elections (COMELEC) resigns, and no new Chairman has been appointed. The President issues a memorandum designating a Commissioner as “Acting Chairman” and says the designation may be revoked at any time. Another Commissioner challenges it. He argues that (a) the President cannot designate an acting head of a Constitutional Commission, and (b) the President's act is only temporary and the designee is already a Commissioner, so it is harmless. Should the challenge be sustained? Explain.
alac: Yes. The challenge should be sustained. The designation is invalid.

Jurisprudence provides that the President cannot designate an acting chairman of a Constitutional Commission, even temporarily. A designation revocable at will makes the officer depend on the President, which destroys the commission's independence. A temporary arrangement is for the Commission itself to decide.

On (a), the Constitution gives the President the power to appoint, with the Commission on Appointments' consent, but not to designate an acting chair. On (b), the designee holds the position at the President's pleasure because the designation can be revoked at any time. That dependence is exactly what harms independence, even for a short time or if the designee is already a Commissioner.
Therefore, the designation is invalid. The Commission may choose who will act as Chairman.
D.key: At-will designation by the President = loss of independence. The Commission picks its own acting head.

D.name: Funa v. Villar (Chairman, COA)
D.hook: Why is the seat empty? Then add up the years — never over 7.
D.rule: Expired term → full 7 years; death/resignation/disability/impeachment → only the leftover term; total service never over 7.
mem: “…for a term of seven years without reappointment… Appointment to any vacancy shall be only for the unexpired portion of the term of the predecessor. In no case shall any Member be appointed or designated in a temporary or acting capacity.” — Art. IX-D, Sec. 1(2)
doc: **Expired** term → next appointment is a **full 7 years**; less is void.
**Death, resignation, disability, impeachment** → only the **unexpired portion**.
Served a full 7 years → **never** reappointed.
No temporary or acting appointment.
**Bar-style tie-in:** two officers resign after exactly 2 of 7 years; the successors fill only the remaining 5 years (until 2030). The Ombudsman point is debatable; verify.
D.drill: Deanna and Lec are best friends in law school. On March 6, 2025, the President appoints Deanna as Ombudsman, after the former Ombudsman resigned having served exactly two years of his seven-year term. On the same day, the President appoints Lec as Chair of the Commission on Audit (COA), after the former Chair resigned also having served exactly two years of his seven-year term. Deanna and Lec both claim that they will serve a full seven years, until 2032. Are they correct? Explain.
alac: No. Neither will serve until 2032. Each will serve only the unexpired portion, until 2030.

Jurisprudence provides that when a term expires, the next appointee serves a full seven years. But when the vacancy arises from death, resignation, disability, or impeachment, the appointee serves only the unexpired portion of the predecessor's term. Total service never goes beyond seven years, and no appointment may be temporary or acting. For Constitutional Commissions, the Constitution says appointment to a vacancy is only for the unexpired portion of the term of the predecessor.

Lec's predecessor resigned, and the vacancy was filled before the term expired, so Lec serves only the remaining five years, until 2030. Deanna's case is an Ombudsman post under Art. XI, not a Commission under Art. IX, and the text on the unexpired portion is stated for the Commissions. But the reasons in Funa, which keep terms staggered and protect independence, apply equally: her predecessor resigned, so she is best seen as serving the five years left. [Beyond the 28 cases: the Ombudsman point is debatable; verify against your notes.]
Therefore, Lec will serve until 2030. Deanna also will serve until 2030, applying the reasoning in Funa, though that point is open to argument.
D.key: Expired term → full seven years. Resignation, death, disability, impeachment → unexpired portion only. Watch whether the post is a Commission (text is express) or the Ombudsman (apply the reasoning).

D.name: CSC v. Pililla Water District
D.hook: Confidence lost = term over (not removal).
D.rule: A water district GM holds a primarily confidential position; courts decide this by the job's nature; loss of confidence ends the term and is not removal.
mem: “Appointments in the civil service shall be made only according to merit and fitness… except to positions which are policy-determining, primarily confidential, or highly technical…” — Art. IX-B, Sec. 2(2)
doc: **Proximity rule:** look at the job's actual functions and closeness to the appointing power.
**Courts**, not the CSC, have the final say.
Loss of confidence = **expiration of term**, not removal.
D.drill: The General Manager (GM) of a local water district is hired by the water district's board on the board's choice. The Civil Service Commission (CSC) says the GM's position is career service and the board may not remove him without cause. Later the board terminates the GM, saying it lost confidence in him. The GM argues that (a) the CSC has already classified the position as career, and (b) he was removed without cause. Is the GM correct? Explain.
alac: No. The GM is not correct.

Jurisprudence provides that a GM of a water district holds a primarily confidential position. Courts, not the CSC, have the final say on whether a position is primarily confidential, and they decide by the nature of the job, using the proximity rule: the actual functions and closeness to the appointing power. Loss of confidence ends the term and is not removal.

On (a), the CSC's label is not binding. The GM works closely with the board and has a close and trusting relationship with it, which makes the position primarily confidential. On (b), the board did not remove him for cause. His term simply ended when confidence was lost, so no cause is needed.
Therefore, the GM's term ended with loss of confidence. He cannot claim to have been removed without cause.
D.key: Job nature + closeness to the appointing power decide, and courts have the last word. Loss of confidence = expiration, not removal.

D.name: Philippine Press Institute v. COMELEC
D.hook: Free newspaper space = taking. Free airtime = OK.
D.rule: COMELEC cannot force newspapers to give free space (taking without just compensation), but broadcasters may be required to give free airtime.
mem: “Private property shall not be taken for public use without just compensation.” — Art. III, Sec. 9
COMELEC may “supervise or regulate the enjoyment or utilization of all franchises or permits…” for media during the election period — Art. IX-C, Sec. 4
doc: Forced donation of print space is **eminent domain without pay**.
Not valid police power — **no necessity** shown.
"Supervise or regulate" does **not** include a power to take.

**Bar-style tie-in:** “Oplan Baklas”: a size limit may be a valid regulation, but forcible entry, confiscation and destruction without notice and hearing is a taking without due process. [Outside the 28 cases; verify.]
D.drill: The COMELEC issues a resolution requiring all newspapers of general circulation to give a fixed amount of free print space to candidates during the campaign. COMELEC says it is regulating the media during the election period and that the space is needed to give candidates an equal chance. A press association challenges the resolution. It argues that (a) the resolution takes private property without just compensation, and (b) COMELEC's power to supervise or regulate media does not include a power to take. Should the challenge succeed? Explain.
alac: Yes. The challenge should succeed as to print media.

Jurisprudence provides that forcing newspapers to donate print space is eminent domain without pay. Private property may not be taken for public use without just compensation. The order is also not valid police power because no necessity was shown. The power to “supervise or regulate” does not include a power to take. Broadcasters, who use public franchises, may be required to give free airtime.

On (a), the space belongs to the newspapers, who sell it. Taking it free for candidates is a taking without payment. On (b), COMELEC's power to supervise or regulate franchises and permits does not reach private newspapers, which operate without a franchise. COMELEC also showed no necessity for the taking.
Therefore, the resolution is invalid as to the newspapers. COMELEC may buy the space, or ask for voluntary donation.
D.key: Print = private property (no free taking). Broadcast = public franchise (free airtime may be required).

D.name: Peñera v. COMELEC
D.hook: Candidate only when the campaign starts.
D.rule: A person who files a COC becomes a candidate only at the start of the campaign period, so acts before it are not premature campaigning.
mem: “Any person who files his certificate of candidacy… shall only be considered as a candidate at the start of the campaign period…” — R.A. 8436, Sec. 15, as amended by R.A. 9369
doc: Unlawful acts that apply to **candidates** take effect only at the start of the campaign period.
The Court **reversed** its Sept. 11, 2009 decision on reconsideration (Nov. 25, 2009).
D.drill: Mayor Pena files her certificate of candidacy (COC) in October for the May election. The campaign period for local officials starts in March. In December, she holds a motorcade and rally with her supporters, and in January she posts ads online asking people to vote for her. A rival asks COMELEC to disqualify her for premature campaigning, since she already filed her COC. Pena says she was not yet a candidate. Is Pena correct? Explain.
alac: Yes. Pena is correct. She cannot be disqualified for premature campaigning.

Jurisprudence provides that 2009, on reconsideration, which reversed the Sept. 11, 2009 decision), a person who files a COC becomes a candidate only at the start of the campaign period. Unlawful acts that apply to candidates take effect only at the start of the campaign period.

Here, Pena filed her COC in October, but the campaign period started only in March. The motorcade in December and the ads in January happened before the campaign period. At that time she was not yet a candidate in the legal sense, so the law on unlawful campaigning did not yet apply.
Therefore, Pena may not be disqualified for premature campaigning.
D.key: COC filing alone does not make one a candidate for campaign-offense purposes. The campaign period does.

D.name: Señeres v. COMELEC
D.hook: Oath taken → go to the HRET.
D.rule: Once party-list nominees are proclaimed, sworn in, and assume office, only the HRET can hear challenges to them.
mem: “The Senate and the House of Representatives shall each have an Electoral Tribunal which shall be the sole judge of all contests relating to the election, returns, and qualifications of their respective Members.” — Art. VI, Sec. 17
doc: **Hold-over:** an officer whose term expired may continue until a successor is elected, unless party rules forbid.
**Estoppel:** one who benefited from an officer's acts cannot later question that officer's authority.
D.drill: A party-list group's nominees are proclaimed winners, sworn in, and take their seats in the House of Representatives. Later, a rival group files a petition in COMELEC to cancel the nominee's nomination, claiming that the nominee was not properly nominated by the party. The nominee also benefited from the party's acts as a hold-over officer of the party. Does COMELEC still have jurisdiction? Explain.
alac: No. COMELEC no longer has jurisdiction. The House of Representatives Electoral Tribunal (HRET) has it.

Jurisprudence provides that once party-list nominees are proclaimed, sworn in, and assume office, only the HRET can hear challenges to them. A hold-over officer whose term expired may continue until a successor is elected, unless party rules forbid. A person who benefited from an officer's acts cannot later question that officer's authority.

Here, the nominees have been proclaimed, sworn in, and have assumed office. The challenge to the nomination is a challenge to their qualifications and belongs to the HRET. In addition, the rival group, which benefited from the acts of the hold-over officer, is estopped from questioning his authority.
Therefore, the petition in COMELEC must be dismissed.
D.key: Proclaimed + oath + assumption = HRET's turf. Estoppel blocks those who benefited from an officer's acts.

D.name: Liberal Party v. COMELEC
D.hook: Register first, accredit after. A deadline is a deadline.
D.rule: A coalition must register before it can be accredited, and registration deadlines are mandatory, including for coalitions.
mem: COMELEC shall “register, after sufficient publication, political parties, organizations, or coalitions…” — Art. IX-C, Sec. 2(5)
doc: Registration is **not** mere recognition of an "operative fact"; it requires discretion and quasi-judicial evaluation.
Granting **late** registration is grave abuse of discretion.
D.drill: A group of three parties forms a coalition for the next election. The coalition does not register by the deadline set by law. COMELEC then grants it late registration, and later accredits it as a coalition for party-list purposes. A rival party challenges. It argues that (a) a coalition must register before it can be accredited, and (b) the late registration is invalid. COMELEC says registration is only the recognition of an operative fact. Should the challenge succeed? Explain.
alac: Yes. The challenge should succeed.

Jurisprudence provides that a coalition must register before it can be accredited. Registration is not mere recognition of an operative fact; it requires discretion and quasi-judicial evaluation. Registration deadlines are mandatory, including for coalitions. Granting late registration is grave abuse of discretion.

On (a), the coalition had not registered before it was accredited, so the accreditation has no basis. On (b), the registration deadline had passed, and it is mandatory. COMELEC's argument that registration only recognizes a fact is wrong because registration involves evaluation.
Therefore, the late registration and the accreditation are invalid, for grave abuse of discretion.
D.key: Registration comes before accreditation; deadlines are mandatory and cannot be waived.

D.name: Galindo v. COA
D.hook: COA as boss → appeal to CSC. Auditors take nothing from auditees.
D.rule: When COA disciplines its own staff, the remedy is appeal to the CSC, not certiorari to the SC; auditors may not take benefits from the agencies they audit.
mem: “…any decision, order, or ruling of each Commission may be brought to the Supreme Court on certiorari… within thirty days…” — Art. IX-A, Sec. 7
doc: Substantial evidence is enough in administrative cases.

**Bar-style tie-in:** an office-issued laptop scanned in a routine replacement gives little room for a privacy claim; the standard in administrative cases is substantial evidence. [Pollo is outside the 28 cases; verify.]
D.drill: A COA staff member is found guilty of grave misconduct by COA after an administrative hearing, on substantial evidence. He files a petition for certiorari in the Supreme Court. He argues that (a) the Supreme Court is the proper forum since COA is a Constitutional Commission, and (b) the evidence was not enough. COA also found that he served as paid consultant to an agency he audited. Should the petition be granted? Explain.
alac: No. The petition should not be granted.

Jurisprudence provides that when COA disciplines its own staff, the remedy is appeal to the Civil Service Commission (CSC), not certiorari to the Supreme Court. Substantial evidence is enough in administrative cases. Auditors may not take benefits from the agencies they audit.

On (a), the staff member went to the wrong forum. The remedy is appeal to the CSC. On (b), substantial evidence, which means relevant evidence a reasonable mind might accept, is enough. Being paid by an agency he audited is a taking of benefits from an audited agency, which an auditor may not do.
Therefore, the petition should be dismissed.
D.key: COA staff discipline → CSC, not SC certiorari. Substantial evidence is enough. Auditors take nothing from the audited.

D.name: BSP v. COA
D.hook: No stock, no members → not a GOCC.
D.rule: The BSP is not a GOCC (no stock, no members), so GOCC laws do not apply to it, but COA still audits it.
mem: “The Congress shall establish an independent central monetary authority…” — Art. XII, Sec. 20
“No law shall be passed exempting any entity of the Government… from the jurisdiction of the Commission on Audit.” — Art. IX-D, Sec. 3
doc: BSP = **instrumentality with corporate powers**, not stock or non-stock.
COA may decide questions of law in an audit, but must apply the **correct law**.
D.drill: COA applies the rules for government-owned and controlled corporations (GOCCs) to the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP). It disallows certain BSP expenses and demands a governance fee. BSP replies that it is not a GOCC, and that COA has no jurisdiction to audit it at all. Who is correct? Explain.
alac: BSP is correct that it is not a GOCC, but COA may still audit BSP.

Jurisprudence provides that the BSP is not a GOCC because it has no stock and no members. It is an instrumentality with corporate powers. GOCC laws therefore do not apply to it. COA may still audit it, and may decide questions of law in an audit, but it must apply the correct law.

Here, COA applied the GOCC rules to BSP, which is the wrong law. The governance fee and disallowances based on GOCC laws cannot stand. But BSP is a government body, so COA still has the power to audit its funds.
Therefore, the GOCC-based disallowances are invalid, but COA's audit authority remains.
D.key: Not a GOCC (no stock, no members) → GOCC laws do not apply. COA still audits, using the correct law.

D.name: MIAA v. City of Pasay
D.hook: Airport is public. The leased part pays tax.
D.rule: MIAA is a government instrumentality; airport property is exempt from real property tax, except parts leased to private persons.
mem: “Each local government unit shall have the power to create its own sources of revenues and to levy taxes… subject to such guidelines and limitations as the Congress may provide…” — Art. X, Sec. 5
doc: Airport lands and buildings are **property of public dominion** owned by the Republic.
D.drill: The City of Pasay assesses real property tax on the airport lands and buildings managed by the Manila International Airport Authority (MIAA). The city also sets the runway and some lots for auction for non-payment. MIAA says it is exempt. The city says MIAA is a corporation and so taxable. Part of the property is leased to a private company. Who is correct? Explain.
alac: MIAA is correct as to the airport property, but the parts leased to private persons are taxable.

Jurisprudence provides that MIAA is a government instrumentality, not a GOCC, and airport lands and buildings are property of public dominion owned by the Republic. They are exempt from real property tax, except parts leased to private persons.

Here, the runway and airport facilities are public dominion property of the Republic, so they cannot be taxed or auctioned. The portions leased to the private company may be taxed because the beneficial use has passed to a private person.
Therefore, the assessment and auction are invalid, except as to the leased portion.
D.key: Public dominion property is not taxable or auctionable; leased-out parts are the exception.

D.name: CHREA v. CHR
D.hook: Only J-C-O have fiscal autonomy.
D.rule: Only the Judiciary, the Constitutional Commissions, and the Ombudsman (J-C-O) have fiscal autonomy; the CHR does not, so it needs DBM approval.
mem: Fiscal autonomy appears only in: Art. VIII, Sec. 3 (Judiciary) · Art. IX-A, Sec. 5 (Commissions) · Art. XI, Sec. 14 (Ombudsman)
doc: **Independent ≠ fiscally autonomous.**
Upgrading or reclassifying positions needs **DBM approval** under the Salary Standardization Law.
D.drill: The Commission on Human Rights (CHR) approves a new staffing pattern and upgrades several positions with higher salaries, without the approval of the Department of Budget and Management (DBM). The CHR says it is an independent body and has fiscal autonomy. DBM refuses to release funds. Who is correct? Explain.
alac: DBM is correct. The CHR does not have fiscal autonomy.

Jurisprudence provides that only the Judiciary, the Constitutional Commissions, and the Ombudsman (J-C-O) have fiscal autonomy. Independent does not mean fiscally autonomous. Upgrading or reclassifying positions needs DBM approval under the Salary Standardization Law.
Here, the CHR is independent, but it is not one of the J-C-O. So its upgrades need DBM approval, which it did not get.
Therefore, the upgrades are invalid without DBM approval.
D.key: J-C-O only. Independent ≠ fiscally autonomous.

TW.label: Fact-finding commission
TW.facts: A newly built government bridge collapses, killing 40 people. The President issues an executive order creating a five-member “Bridge Collapse Commission” to investigate and recommend charges to the DOJ. The commission may subpoena documents, but it has no power to punish anyone. No law authorizes the commission. The contractors argue that only Congress can create public offices, so the order is void.
TW.q: Is the executive order valid? Explain.
TW.hint: Is the commission deciding cases, or only finding facts and recommending?
alac: Yes. The executive order creating the commission is valid.

The Constitution vests the executive power in the President and requires the President to ensure that the laws are faithfully executed. Jurisprudence provides that executive power is broader than the powers listed. The President may create ad hoc fact-finding bodies to gather facts and recommend action, as long as these bodies do not decide cases or exercise powers that belong to Congress or the courts.

Here, the commission only investigates the collapse and recommends charges to the DOJ. It does not try anyone or impose penalties. This means it is a tool the President uses to see that the laws on public works and safety are carried out, not a new office with powers of its own.
Therefore, the contractors are wrong. The executive order is valid.
TW.key: A fact-finding body that only investigates and recommends is within executive power. If it starts deciding cases or punishing people, it crosses into judicial power.

TW.label: State of national emergency
TW.facts: After a series of bombings in three cities, the President issues a proclamation declaring a “state of national emergency” and orders the AFP and PNP to suppress lawless violence. Several newspapers say the proclamation allows warrantless arrests and takeover of private radio stations. No law requires or authorizes such a declaration. Opposition legislators argue that the President cannot declare something the Constitution does not mention. Is the proclamation valid? Explain.
TW.hint: Does the declaration give the President any new power, or only describe the situation?
alac: Yes, as to the declaration and the order to the AFP and PNP. No, as to any takeover of private radio stations or any warrantless arrests that the proclamation might be read to allow.

The Constitution vests the executive power in the President and makes the President the Commander-in-Chief, who may call out the armed forces to suppress lawless violence. Jurisprudence provides that the President's powers are not limited to those listed. A declaration of a state of emergency is valid when it only describes the situation and adds no new powers. But the President cannot use it to take over private businesses or suspend rights without a law or the steps the Constitution requires.

Here, the bombings show real lawless violence, so there is a factual basis. The proclamation describes the situation and directs the AFP and PNP to act, which the President may do already. But taking over private radio stations needs a law, and warrantless arrests are allowed only in the cases already permitted by the Rules of Court.
Therefore, the proclamation is valid insofar as it only describes the emergency and calls out the armed forces. Any added power to take over stations or arrest without a warrant is void.
TW.key: A declaration that only describes a crisis is valid. But it cannot add powers: takeovers and suspension of rights need a law or the specific steps in the Constitution.

TW.label: Officials barred from Congress (EO 111)
TW.facts: The Senate Blue Ribbon Committee investigates charges of corruption against some executive officials. Citing the President's residual powers and the principle of separation of powers, the President issues Executive Order No. 111. It lists the officials covered by executive privilege and prohibits them from appearing before any congressional inquiry without the President's prior approval. The Senate petitions the Supreme Court. Is E.O. 111 unconstitutional? Explain.
TW.hint: Residual power fills gaps in executive action. Can it override a power the Constitution gives Congress?
alac: Yes, as to the blanket prohibition. E.O. 111 is unconstitutional insofar as it bars officials from appearing in inquiries in aid of legislation without prior approval.

Jurisprudence provides that the President has residual powers, but these cannot be used to override another branch's constitutional power. The Constitution gives Congress the power to conduct inquiries in aid of legislation, and appearance in these inquiries is compulsory. Jurisprudence provides that prior consent was required only for the question hour, and executive privilege must be invoked by the President or the Executive Secretary on specific grounds. [Beyond the 28 cases: check this against your own notes.]

Here, E.O. 111 requires prior approval for all inquiries and lists officials covered by executive privilege in advance. This gives the President a blanket power to block Congress, not a case-by-case assertion of privilege with stated reasons. A residual power cannot be used to limit a power the Constitution gives to Congress.
Therefore, E.O. 111 is unconstitutional as to inquiries in aid of legislation. The prior-approval rule may be valid only for the question hour.
TW.key: TWIST: residual power cannot cut into another branch's power. Appearance in inquiries in aid of legislation is compulsory; privilege is claimed case by case with reasons. [Senate v. Ermita is outside the 28 cases; verify.]

TW.label: Congress limits pardon
TW.facts: Congress passes a law saying that no pardon may be granted to a person convicted of graft until at least ten years after conviction and unless a Board of Pardons has recommended it. The President, after a graft conviction became final, grants an absolute pardon to a former governor eight years later. The former governor now runs for Congress. A voter argues that the pardon is void for violating the law. Is the pardon valid? Explain.
TW.hint: Can a law narrow a power the Constitution gives to the President?
alac: Yes. The pardon is valid.
The Constitution gives the President the power to grant pardons after conviction by final judgment. Jurisprudence provides that the pardoning power is plenary and Congress cannot add limits by law.

Here, the conviction was already final when the pardon was granted. The ten-year wait and the Board recommendation are limits imposed by Congress on a power the Constitution gives the President, so they cannot bind the President.
Therefore, the pardon is valid. The voter is wrong.
TW.key: Congress cannot make limits on the pardoning power. Only the Constitution (e.g. final conviction, no pardon in impeachment cases, no pardon for election offenses without COMELEC's recommendation) limits it.

TW.label: No Board recommendation
TW.facts: The President grants an executive clemency to a convict without waiting for the Board of Pardons and Parole to make a recommendation. The pardon says the convict is “restored to his civil and political rights.” An opponent argues that the pardon is invalid because it skipped the Board and because the pardon was only granted after the convict had served only half of his sentence. Is the opponent correct? Explain.
TW.hint: Who sets the process for the pardoning power, the Constitution or an agency's rules?
alac: No. The opponent is wrong. The pardon is valid.

The pardoning power of the President is plenary. Jurisprudence provides that it is subject only to limits in the Constitution, and it cannot be controlled by Congress. The Board of Pardons and Parole is an adviser and its recommendation is not a constitutional requirement.

Here, the Constitution does not require a Board recommendation or service of a minimum part of the sentence. The pardon also expressly restores civil and political rights, so the convict's disqualification is lifted.
Therefore, the pardon is valid.
TW.key: The Board advises; it does not control. A pardon with express restoration of civil and political rights restores the right to run.

TW.label: Pardon while appeal is pending
TW.facts: A mayor is convicted of malversation by the Sandiganbayan. He appeals to the Supreme Court. While the appeal is pending, the President grants him an absolute pardon, and the mayor files his certificate of candidacy for governor. A rival argues that the pardon is void. Is the rival correct? Explain.
TW.hint: What does the Constitution require before the President may pardon?
alac: Yes. The pardon is void.

The Constitution allows the President to grant pardon only after conviction by final judgment. Jurisprudence provides that the pardoning power is plenary, but it still operates within this constitutional limit.
Here, the mayor's appeal is still pending, so the conviction is not yet final. The pardon is premature and so the mayor stays disqualified and the rival is right.
Therefore, the pardon is void.
TW.key: TWIST: plenary does not mean limitless. The Constitution requires final judgment first. The mayor may withdraw the appeal and then seek a new pardon.

TW.label: Amnesty without Congress
TW.facts: The President issues a proclamation granting amnesty to rebels who surrender within sixty days. Congress has not passed any resolution. Some rebels surrender and ask that their cases be dismissed. A prosecutor refuses, arguing that the amnesty is invalid. The rebels respond that the President is the chief executive and may grant amnesty. Who is correct? Explain.
TW.hint: Who must join the President for an amnesty to take effect?
alac: No. The amnesty is invalid. The prosecutor is correct.
The Constitution requires the concurrence of a majority of all the Members of Congress for amnesty. Jurisprudence provides that amnesty is a joint act of the President and Congress.
Here, the proclamation was issued with no concurrence from Congress. The President alone cannot grant amnesty. Being the chief executive does not give the President this power.
Therefore, the amnesty is invalid and the cases need not be dismissed.
TW.key: Pardon is the President's alone; amnesty needs the President plus a majority of all Members of Congress.

TW.label: Mass revocation without hearing
TW.facts: Congress concurred in an amnesty for 200 former rebels. Two years later, the President issues a proclamation revoking the amnesty of all 200 because some of them allegedly lied in their applications. The proclamation orders all 200 to be arrested at once, with no notice to them. Can the President do this? Explain.
TW.hint: Even if some people did wrong, can all of them lose their amnesty at once and unheard?
alac: No. The revocation is invalid.
Jurisprudence provides that amnesty needs the concurrence of Congress, so the President cannot revoke it alone. Revoking a granted amnesty without notice and hearing also violates due process.

Here, the President revoked all 200 amnesties alone and without giving notice or a hearing to anyone. Even if some lied, that must be shown for each person. Those who did not lie lose a vested benefit without being heard.
Therefore, the revocation is invalid.
TW.key: Revocation fails on two grounds: the President acted alone, and there was no individual notice and hearing.

TW.label: Conditional pardon revoked
TW.facts: The President grants a conditional pardon to a convict, with the condition that he must not commit another crime. Later, the President is told that the convict has violated this condition. Without giving him a hearing, the President orders his arrest to serve the rest of his sentence. The convict relies on Trillanes and argues that the revocation needs Congress and a hearing. Is the convict correct? Explain.
TW.hint: Is a pardon a joint act like amnesty?
alac: No. The convict is wrong on the need for Congress. He may be right only if the revocation was arbitrary.

A pardon is the act of the President alone, while amnesty needs Congress. Jurisprudence provides that revocation by the President alone is barred only for amnesty, because amnesty is a joint act. Under the Revised Administrative Code and settled jurisprudence, the President may determine that a condition of a conditional pardon has been violated and may order arrest. [Beyond the 28 cases: check this against your notes.]

Here, this is a pardon, not an amnesty, so Congress is not needed. The President may decide that the condition was breached without first hearing the convict. The convict may still go to court if the finding is baseless.
Therefore, the convict is wrong. Trillanes does not apply to conditional pardons.
TW.key: TWIST: Trillanes protects amnesty, not pardons. A conditional pardon can be revoked by the President alone. [Verify the no-hearing rule against your notes.]

TW.label: Withdrawal from a plain treaty
TW.facts: The Philippines is a party to a trade treaty that the Senate concurred in. The treaty has no implementing law in the Philippines. The Senate's concurrence said nothing about withdrawal. The President gives notice of withdrawal after the treaty began to hurt local farmers. A farmers' group sues, arguing that the Senate must agree to the withdrawal. Is the withdrawal valid? Explain.
TW.hint: Did the Senate attach any condition, or did a later law implement the treaty?
alac: Yes. The withdrawal is valid.

The President is the primary architect of foreign policy and may withdraw from a treaty. Jurisprudence provides that the power is not absolute: it cannot be used if the Senate made its concurrence depend on its consent to withdrawal, or if a later law implements the treaty.
Here, the Senate attached no condition on withdrawal, and no law implements the treaty. Neither exception applies.
Therefore, the withdrawal is valid.
TW.key: Run both exceptions every time: (1) Senate condition on withdrawal, (2) implementing law.

TW.label: Senators sue on their own
TW.facts: The President withdraws from a treaty. Three senators who voted for the treaty file a petition in their own names to nullify the withdrawal. They say they have a stake because their votes in the Senate are made meaningless. The Senate as a body has passed no resolution on the matter. Will the petition prosper? Explain.
TW.hint: Whose injury is it: the Senate's or the individual senators'?
alac: No. The petition will not prosper because the senators lack standing.
Jurisprudence provides that senators suing individually lack standing if the Senate as a body passed no resolution. Any injury to the power to concur belongs to the Senate as an institution.
Here, the senators sue in their own names, and the Senate passed no resolution objecting to the withdrawal. They claim an injury to their votes, but that is an injury to the Senate.
Therefore, the petition should be dismissed for lack of standing.
TW.key: The institution's injury needs the institution's action (a Senate resolution).

TW.label: Treaty backed by a later law
TW.facts: The Philippines ratified a treaty on environmental protection with the Senate's concurrence. Congress later passed a law that adopts the treaty's rules as national law and creates agencies to enforce it. The President then withdraws from the treaty without asking Congress. Environmental groups sue. The Solicitor General says that the President can always withdraw from treaties. Who is correct? Explain.
TW.hint: Which exception to the President's power is in play?
alac: No. The withdrawal is invalid, or at least cannot undo the law.

Jurisprudence provides that the President may withdraw from a treaty, but not when a later law implements the treaty. In that case, withdrawal would amount to undoing a statute, which only Congress may do.

Here, Congress passed a law that adopts the treaty's rules and sets up enforcement agencies. A withdrawal by the President alone would defeat that law. The Solicitor General's blanket statement ignores this exception.
Therefore, the withdrawal is invalid.
TW.key: TWIST: the President's power to withdraw ends where a later statute implements the treaty.

TW.label: Suit to bare a loan deal
TW.facts: A citizens' group asks the court to order the Finance Department to release the full loan agreement the Philippines signed with a foreign bank for a highway project. The government refuses, saying that the agreement has a clause that the terms are confidential, and that disclosure would hurt future negotiations. Should the court order disclosure? Explain.
TW.q: Should the court order disclosure? Explain.
TW.hint: Can a contract clause defeat a constitutional right to information?
alac: Yes. The court should order disclosure.
Jurisprudence provides that confidentiality clauses cannot defeat the right to information on foreign loans. Information on foreign loans must be made public.
Here, the government relies only on a confidentiality clause and a general worry about future negotiations. A private contract cannot cancel a right the Constitution gives.
Therefore, the court should order the release of the agreement.
TW.key: A contract clause cannot override a constitutional right to information.

TW.label: Damages for acts before office
TW.facts: Before becoming President, Mr. Reyes was a mayor and allegedly signed a contract that harmed a contractor. The contractor sues him for damages while he is the sitting President. Mr. Reyes asks for dismissal on the ground of presidential immunity. The contractor says the act happened before he became President. Who is correct? Explain.
TW.q: Should the suit against the sitting President be dismissed? Explain.
TW.hint: Does immunity depend on when the act happened?
alac: Yes. The suit against the sitting President should be dismissed.
Jurisprudence provides that a sitting President cannot be sued in any case, whatever the case. The immunity covers the person during the term, not only official acts.
Here, the contractor sues Mr. Reyes while he is President. The timing of the act is not relevant, because the protection is for the time of the suit.
Therefore, the suit must be dismissed as to the sitting President, though it may be refiled after the term ends.
TW.key: Immunity attaches to the sitting President for all cases. It does not erase the claim; it only delays it.
