TW.label: Suit after the term ends
TW.facts: A former President's term ended last month. A taxpayer files a suit questioning a foreign loan that the former President approved while in office. The former President argues that presidential immunity bars the suit. The taxpayer says the loan lacked the Monetary Board's concurrence. Does immunity apply? Explain.
TW.q: Does presidential immunity bar the suit? Explain.
TW.hint: Immunity is for the sitting President. What changed?
alac: No. Immunity does not bar the suit once the term has ended.
Jurisprudence provides that the immunity applies to a sitting President. It ends when the term ends.

Here, the former President is no longer in office. The suit is filed after the term ended, so the immunity cannot be invoked. The question will be whether the loan had the Monetary Board's concurrence, as the Constitution requires.
Therefore, the immunity is gone, and the suit may proceed.
TW.key: TWIST: immunity belongs to the sitting President only. After the term, claims can be filed.

TW.label: Oath after the ban starts
TW.facts: The election ban starts on March 9. On March 5, the President signs an appointment and the papers are delivered to the appointee on March 6. On March 7 the appointee accepts in writing but takes the oath of office and assumes duty only on March 12. The appointee says the appointment was complete before the ban. Is the appointee correct? Explain.
TW.hint: Count all four steps: sign, transmit, receive, accept (oath and assumption).
alac: No. The appointment is void.
Jurisprudence provides that appointment is a process with four steps, and all must be finished before the ban begins. Acceptance is shown by oath and assumption of duties.
Here, the oath and the assumption happened on March 12, after the ban began on March 9. So the fourth step was not complete in time.
Therefore, the appointment is void.
TW.key: Acceptance (oath and assumption) is the last step. If it comes after the ban, the appointment fails.

TW.label: Position not yet vacant
TW.facts: On February 20, the President signs an appointment to a position that will become vacant on March 1, when the incumbent retires. The appointee takes the oath on March 3 and assumes duty on March 10, when the ban is already running. Is the appointment valid? Explain.
TW.hint: The ban is counted from the finishing of the whole process.
alac: No. The appointment is void.
Jurisprudence provides that an appointment is a process and every step must be done before the ban. The appointee must also have accepted before the ban.

Here, assumption of duty occurred on March 10, within the ban period. Signing in February does not save the appointment. The vacancy arising only on March 1 also shows the appointment was made in advance of the post being vacant.
Therefore, the appointment is void.
TW.key: An early signature does not complete the process. The ban date controls.

TW.label: Temporary appointment in a crisis
TW.facts: During the ban, the head of the national disaster agency dies right before a super typhoon. The President immediately appoints a temporary head, saying that without one the agency cannot manage the relief operation. A candidate sues, saying all appointments are banned during the period. Is the appointment valid? Explain.
TW.q: Is the temporary appointment valid? Explain.
TW.hint: Does the ban have any exception?
alac: Yes. The temporary appointment is valid.
Jurisprudence provides that the ban has an exception for temporary appointments to executive positions when continued vacancies will prejudice public service or endanger public safety.
Here, a typhoon is coming and the agency has no head. A vacancy in this position endangers public safety, and the appointment is only temporary.
Therefore, the appointment is valid.
TW.key: TWIST: the exception covers temporary appointments where vacancy would hurt public service or safety. Permanent appointments do not fit.

TW.label: RTC judge during the ban
TW.facts: During the ban, the President appoints a new Regional Trial Court judge from the JBC's shortlist to fill a vacancy. A losing applicant sues, arguing that the ban covers all appointments. Is the appointment valid? Explain.
TW.hint: Where is the ban found in the Constitution?
alac: Yes. The appointment is valid.
Jurisprudence provides that the ban is found in the article on the Executive Department, so it covers only the Executive Department. The JBC process already prevents the abuses the ban targets.
Here, an RTC judge is in the Judiciary. The ban does not apply, and the appointee came from the JBC's list.
Therefore, the appointment is valid.
TW.key: The ban reaches the Executive Department only. Judiciary appointments follow the JBC process.

TW.label: Supreme Court seat and the 90 days
TW.facts: A Justice retires during the ban. The President delays making an appointment until after the ban ends, saying that the 90-day period is just a guide. The vacancy goes beyond 90 days. A lawyer sues. Is the delay allowed? Explain.
TW.hint: Is the word in Art. VIII, Sec. 4(1) “shall” or “may”?
alac: No. The delay is not allowed.
Jurisprudence provides that the 90-day period to fill Supreme Court vacancies is mandatory because the Constitution says “shall.” The ban does not apply to the Judiciary.
Here, the ban is not a ground to delay. The President was required to fill the vacancy within 90 days.
Therefore, the delay violates the Constitution.
TW.key: “Shall” means mandatory, and the ban is not an excuse.

TW.label: Executive post during the ban
TW.facts: During the ban, the President appoints a new undersecretary of a department, not as a temporary post. A group sues, citing De Castro and saying that the Court allowed appointments during the ban. Is the appointment valid? Explain.
TW.hint: What did De Castro actually say the ban covers?
alac: No. The appointment is void.

The ban is found in the article on the Executive Department and applies only to it. Jurisprudence provides that only Judiciary appointments are outside the ban. There is an exception for temporary appointments to executive positions when continued vacancies would prejudice public service or endanger public safety.
Here, an undersecretary is an executive post and the appointment is not temporary. De Castro does not help because it dealt only with the Judiciary.
Therefore, the appointment is void.
TW.key: TWIST: De Castro frees only the Judiciary from the ban. Executive posts remain banned except for the narrow exception.

TW.label: Oversight committee approves realignment
TW.facts: The annual budget law says that savings in the budget may be used only for projects that a joint congressional oversight committee approves after the law takes effect. The committee approves the use of savings for ten new projects proposed by individual members. The Executive Secretary argues that Congress may supervise how the budget is spent. Is the oversight committee provision valid? Explain.
TW.hint: Does Congress get a role after it passes the law?
alac: No. The provision is invalid.
Jurisprudence provides that legislators cannot control funds after the budget is passed. Once the budget is enacted, execution belongs to the Executive.
Here, the committee approves the use of savings after the law is passed. This is Congress taking part in execution.
Therefore, the provision is unconstitutional.
TW.key: Congress makes the law; it does not manage the money after it passes.

TW.label: “Such other purposes as the President may determine”
TW.facts: A budget law gives a lump sum to the President “to be used for infrastructure, health, and such other purposes as the President may direct.” The President uses part of it for a new sports facility. A taxpayer sues. Is the phrase valid? Explain.
TW.q: Is the phrase “such other purposes as the President may direct” valid? Explain.
TW.hint: Check both delegation tests: completeness and sufficient standard.
alac: No. The phrase is invalid.
Jurisprudence provides that delegation is valid only if it passes the completeness test and the sufficient standard test. A phrase that lets the President choose any purpose gives no standard.
Here, “such other purposes as the President may direct” is open-ended, so the law is not complete and gives no limits. The President may spend on anything.
Therefore, the phrase is an undue delegation and is unconstitutional.
TW.key: Open-ended discretion on purposes = no sufficient standard.

TW.label: Senator inserts projects before passage
TW.facts: Before the budget bill is passed, a senator persuades the committee to add 20 specific flood control projects, each with an amount and a location, to the bill. The bill is passed and the President signs it. The projects are later found to be overpriced. A group sues to void the law, citing Belgica. Is the law void on the ground in Belgica? Explain.
TW.q: Is the law void under Belgica? Explain.
TW.hint: When was the insertion made: before or after passage?
alac: No, not under Belgica. The insertion by itself is not the ground of Belgica.

Jurisprudence provides that legislators cannot control funds after the budget is passed; the Court struck down legislators' control of funds after the budget was passed. A specific amount for a specific purpose written into the law before passage is an item, which the President may veto or approve.

Here, the projects were written into the bill before passage with amounts and locations. They are items in the law, and the President signed it. Overpricing may mean wrongdoing in implementation, which is a separate issue.
Therefore, the law is not void under Belgica. Officials involved in overpricing may still be held liable.
TW.key: TWIST: the problem in Belgica is control after passage. Items inserted before passage are subject to veto.

TW.label: Ombudsman short on practice years
TW.facts: The Ombudsman is appointed and the Constitution requires at least ten years of practice of law. A citizen shows that the Ombudsman had only six years of practice. The Ombudsman says he can be removed only by impeachment. The Solicitor General files a quo warranto case. Will it prosper? Explain.
TW.hint: Is the challenge about conduct in office or about eligibility?
alac: Yes. Quo warranto will prosper.

Jurisprudence provides that “may” in Under the Constitution, is permissive, so impeachment is not the only way to remove an impeachable officer who was not eligible. The one-year period does not run against the State.
Here, the question is whether the Ombudsman had the required years of practice at appointment. This is eligibility, not misconduct in office.
Therefore, quo warranto will prosper.
TW.key: Eligibility defects → quo warranto. Misconduct in office → impeachment.

TW.label: COMELEC chair who just ran
TW.facts: A person is appointed COMELEC Chair although he was a candidate in the last elections, which the Constitution bars (a candidate in the immediately preceding election cannot be appointed). Two years later, the Solicitor General files a quo warranto. The Chair says that the one-year limit has passed. Is the Chair correct? Explain.
TW.hint: Does the one-year period run against the State?
alac: No. The Chair is wrong.
Jurisprudence provides that the one-year period for quo warranto does not run against the State. Quo warranto is the way to challenge an officer's eligibility.
Here, the Solicitor General filed on behalf of the State. The Chair was not eligible at appointment, so the time limit is no defense.
Therefore, the quo warranto will proceed.
TW.key: State vs private party: prescription does not run against the State.

TW.label: Justice takes bribes in office
TW.facts: A Justice who was properly appointed and qualified is later shown to have accepted bribes while in office. The Solicitor General files quo warranto to oust her. Will it prosper? Explain.
TW.hint: Was the Justice ineligible at appointment?
alac: No. Quo warranto will not prosper. The proper remedy is impeachment.
Jurisprudence provides that quo warranto is for officers who were not eligible when appointed. Bribery during office is a wrong in office, which is a ground for impeachment.
Here, the Justice was qualified when appointed. The bribes came afterwards.
Therefore, quo warranto is the wrong remedy. Impeachment applies.
TW.key: TWIST: Sereno does not turn every wrong into quo warranto. It covers eligibility at the start only.

TW.label: Anonymous bribery letter
TW.facts: The JBC receives an anonymous letter saying an applicant took a bribe as a judge. The JBC removes his name from the shortlist without telling him about the letter or letting him respond. He petitions the Supreme Court. Should the petition be granted? Explain.
TW.q: Should the petition be granted? Explain.
TW.hint: Is the integrity of the applicant challenged?
alac: Yes. The petition should be granted.
Jurisprudence provides that due process applies when the JBC questions an applicant's integrity. The applicant must receive notice and a hearing.
Here, a bribery charge goes to integrity. The applicant was not told and not heard.
Therefore, the exclusion is invalid. He must be given notice and a hearing.
TW.key: Integrity question → notice and hearing, even if the source is anonymous.

TW.label: Disagreement over a dissent
TW.facts: An applicant, as a Court of Appeals Justice, wrote a dissent that some JBC members consider wrong. One member objects and says this shows poor integrity. The JBC applies its unanimity rule and removes the applicant. Is the removal valid? Explain.
TW.hint: Is a disagreement on legal views an integrity issue?
alac: No. The removal is invalid.
Jurisprudence provides that the unanimity rule applies only to integrity questions, not to disagreements about legal strategy or legal views.
Here, the objection is about the quality of a dissent. This is a matter of legal opinion, not of integrity.
Therefore, the unanimity rule does not apply. The removal is invalid.
TW.key: A wrong legal view is not a lack of integrity.

TW.label: Charges given, hearing held
TW.facts: The JBC tells an applicant of the charge that he hid a case, gives him time to answer, and holds a hearing. One member still votes against him on integrity, so the JBC excludes him. The applicant says he was denied due process because he lost anyway. Is he correct? Explain.
TW.hint: What does due process require: a win, or a chance to be heard?
alac: No. The applicant is wrong.
Jurisprudence provides that due process requires notice and a hearing when the integrity of an applicant is challenged. It does not guarantee a favorable result.
Here, he got notice of the charge and a hearing. A member still doubted his integrity and the unanimity rule applies to integrity questions.
Therefore, there was no denial of due process, and the exclusion is valid.
TW.key: TWIST: due process = fair procedure, not a guaranteed result.

TW.label: Exam and training scores
TW.facts: The JBC requires all applicants to pass a written test and to have attended a judicial training program. An applicant who did not attend argues that the JBC cannot add requirements to those in the Constitution. The JBC published its policy. Is the requirement valid? Explain.
TW.hint: Is the JBC adding a qualification or measuring competence?
alac: Yes. The requirement is valid.
Jurisprudence provides that the JBC may set additional standards to measure “proven competence” beyond the minimum constitutional qualifications, if reasonable and published.
Here, the test and the training measure competence, and the policy was published.
Therefore, the requirement is valid.
TW.key: Reasonable + published + measures a constitutional trait = valid.

TW.label: Pending administrative cases
TW.facts: The JBC adopts and publishes a rule that applicants with pending administrative cases are not considered. An applicant with a pending complaint says he has a vested right to be nominated. Is he correct? Explain.
TW.hint: Does anyone have a right to be nominated?
alac: No. The applicant is wrong.
Jurisprudence provides that applicants have no vested right to be nominated. The JBC may set reasonable standards on integrity, if published.
Here, the rule is related to integrity and was published. A pending case is a reasonable ground to hold back consideration.
Therefore, the rule is valid and the applicant has no vested right.
TW.key: No vested right to be nominated.

TW.label: Only three law schools
TW.facts: The JBC adopts and publishes a rule that only graduates of three named law schools may be nominated. A graduate of another school sues, saying this violates equal protection. Is the rule valid? Explain.
TW.hint: Is the classification related to competence?
alac: No. The rule is invalid.

Jurisprudence provides that the five-year rule was valid because experience is a reasonable classification related to competence. Equal protection requires a classification to be based on real differences and related to the purpose.
Here, the school of graduation is not related to competence. Graduates of other schools who passed the bar are equally qualified.
Therefore, the rule violates equal protection.
TW.key: TWIST: only reasonable classifications pass. Experience yes; school name, no.

TW.label: Law expands the JBC to nine
TW.facts: Congress passes a law increasing the JBC to nine members by adding two more representatives of Congress. An applicant says the law is valid because Congress has the power to pass laws. Is the law valid? Explain.
TW.hint: Can a statute change the composition set by the Constitution?
alac: No. The law is invalid.
Jurisprudence provides that the Constitution's composition of the JBC must be read by its plain meaning. Seven members is deliberate to avoid deadlock.
Here, a statute cannot change the composition fixed by the Constitution.
Therefore, the law is invalid.
TW.key: A statute cannot change the Constitution's JBC.

TW.label: Attack on old nominations
TW.facts: After the Court rules that only one representative of Congress sits on the JBC, a losing applicant sues to void all nominations made while two representatives sat. Will the suit prosper? Explain.
TW.hint: What does the operative fact doctrine protect?
alac: No. The suit will not prosper.
Jurisprudence provides that past acts remain valid under the operative fact doctrine.
Here, the nominations were made in reliance on the earlier practice.
Therefore, they stay valid.
TW.key: Operative fact: past acts relied on in good faith stay valid.

TW.label: Senate and House take turns
TW.facts: The Senate and House agree that each chamber will send a representative to the JBC on alternating years, so there is still only one member at a time. A group says this violates the plain meaning of “a representative.” Is the arrangement valid? Explain.
TW.hint: How many members of Congress sit at one time?
alac: Yes, at least in terms of the number. The arrangement is not barred by Chavez on its face.
Jurisprudence provides that “a representative” means one. The seven-member JBC is deliberate.
Here, only one member of Congress sits at any one time, so the number is respected. The Court in Chavez rejected splitting a vote between two members.
Therefore, the rotation does not violate the rule on number, though the arrangement must still not split a vote between two persons.
TW.key: TWIST: the rule is about how many sit at once. [Check this against your notes on how Congress chooses its representative.]

TW.label: Two Supreme Court seats at once
TW.facts: Two seats in the Supreme Court are vacant at the same time. The JBC sends one list of seven nominees. The President wants to choose any two. A petitioner says each vacancy needs its own list of three. Is the petitioner correct? Explain.
TW.hint: Is the rule three per vacancy or a combined list?
alac: No. The petitioner is wrong.

Jurisprudence provides that three per vacancy is met if the combined list has at least three times the number of vacancies, and the JBC cannot cluster nominees for vacancies that exist at the same time.
Here, two vacancies need at least six nominees, and the JBC sent seven.
Therefore, the list is enough and the President may choose any two.
TW.key: 3 × vacancies on one combined list.

TW.label: Fight over seniority
TW.facts: The President appoints three Justices to the Court on three different days within the same week. The last appointed had a longer career in the lower court. He claims to be senior. Is he correct? Explain.
TW.hint: What determines seniority in the same court?
alac: No. He is wrong.
Jurisprudence provides that seniority follows the order of appointment.
Here, he was appointed last, so he is the most junior.
Therefore, his claim fails.
TW.key: Order of appointment decides seniority, not career length.

TW.label: Vacancies at different times
TW.facts: Two vacancies occur months apart. The JBC sends a list of 3 for the first and, months later, a list of 3 for the second. A petitioner cites Aguinaldo and says the JBC cannot send separate lists. Is the petitioner correct? Explain.
TW.hint: Do the vacancies exist at the same time?
alac: No. The petitioner is wrong.
Jurisprudence provides that clustering is barred only for vacancies that exist at the same time.
Here, the vacancies arose at different times, so separate lists of three are the usual process.
Therefore, separate lists are valid.
TW.key: TWIST: the anti-clustering rule applies only to simultaneous vacancies.

TW.label: Retiring judges buy service cars
TW.facts: The Court adopts guidelines letting retiring judges buy their service vehicles at an appraised value computed by the Court. COA says that the value must follow its formula and rejects the Court's guidelines. Is COA correct? Explain.
TW.hint: Who sets the guidelines for the Court's property?
alac: No. COA is wrong.
Jurisprudence provides that fiscal autonomy lets the Court dispose of its own property under its own guidelines. COA still audits but may not force its formula.
Here, the Court's guidelines govern the sale.
Therefore, COA cannot impose its formula.
TW.key: COA audits; it does not set the Court's valuation.

TW.label: Disposal of old court equipment
TW.facts: The Court sells old computers by negotiated sale under its own guidelines. COA disallows the sale because no public bidding was done under COA rules. Is COA correct? Explain.
TW.hint: Is COA auditing or controlling how the Court disposes of its property?
alac: No. COA is wrong to disallow merely because its own rules were not followed.
Fiscal autonomy includes disposing of property under the Court's own guidelines. COA may audit for correctness but cannot dictate the method.
Here, the Court followed its own guidelines.
Therefore, the disallowance is improper unless the Court's own guidelines were not followed.
TW.key: Audit against the Court's own guidelines.

TW.label: Court refuses a regular audit
TW.facts: The Court refuses to let COA audit its funds at all, citing fiscal autonomy. Is the refusal valid? Explain.
TW.hint: Does fiscal autonomy exempt the Court from audit?
alac: No. The refusal is invalid.
COA may still audit the Judiciary. Fiscal autonomy is about flexibility in using funds, not exemption from audit.
Here, the Court cannot refuse an audit.
Therefore, the Court must submit to audit.
TW.key: TWIST: fiscal autonomy does not mean no audit.

TW.label: Bill to abolish a court
TW.facts: A bill is filed in Congress to abolish a specialized court. The judges of that court petition the Supreme Court to stop the bill. Should the Court act? Explain.
TW.hint: Is there an actual case?
alac: No. The Court should not act.
Jurisprudence provides that courts cannot review a proposed bill because there is no actual case yet.
Here, the bill is only a proposal.
Therefore, the petition should be dismissed.
TW.key: No actual case for a mere bill.

TW.label: Pending charter-change resolution
TW.facts: A resolution to amend the judiciary provisions of the Constitution is pending in Congress. Lawyers petition the Court to declare it unconstitutional now. Should the Court act? Explain.
TW.hint: Has the proposal been acted on yet?
alac: No. The Court should not act.
Judicial power requires an actual case. Jurisprudence provides that the Court does not review proposals before they take effect.
Here, the resolution is pending only.
Therefore, the petition is premature.
TW.key: Wait for something real to happen.

TW.label: The bill becomes law (lower burden of proof)
TW.facts: Congress passes, and the President signs, a law lowering the standard of proof for crimes involving infrastructure corruption from proof beyond reasonable doubt to preponderance of evidence. An accused is charged under the law and challenges it. Is the law valid? Explain.
TW.hint: Now there is a real case. What does the Constitution presume about an accused?
alac: No. The law is invalid.

Now that the law is applied to a real accused, there is an actual case that the Court may decide. Jurisprudence provides that courts decide only actual cases, not proposed bills. The Constitution presumes the accused innocent until proved guilty, which requires proof beyond reasonable doubt. [Beyond the 28 cases: verify this point against your notes.] The Supreme Court's rule-making power also may not diminish substantive rights.
Here, a lower standard like preponderance of evidence would allow conviction on less proof, which defeats the presumption of innocence. A rule amendment would have the same defect.
Therefore, the law is unconstitutional, whether made by statute or rule.
TW.key: TWIST: once the law is applied there is a case. The presumption of innocence needs proof beyond reasonable doubt.

TW.label: Clerk resigns mid-case
TW.facts: A clerk of court is charged with misconduct. While the case is pending, the clerk resigns. The clerk asks for dismissal because he is no longer in service. Should it be dismissed? Explain.
TW.q: Should the case be dismissed? Explain.
TW.hint: When did jurisdiction attach?
alac: No. The case should not be dismissed.
Jurisprudence provides that jurisdiction attaches when the complaint is filed while the respondent is in office. Resignation does not end it.
Here, the complaint was filed while the clerk was in office.
Therefore, the case continues.
TW.key: Resignation does not end the case.

TW.label: Judge dies while case pending
TW.facts: A judge dies while an administrative case is pending. His family asks that the case be dismissed. Should it be? Explain.
TW.q: Should the case be dismissed? Explain.
TW.hint: What is the rule on death?
alac: Yes. The case is generally dismissed.
Jurisprudence provides that death generally ends the case, unlike retirement or resignation.
Here, the respondent is dead.
Therefore, the case is generally dismissed.
TW.key: Death generally ends it; retirement and resignation do not.

TW.label: House cites CA Justices in contempt
TW.facts: The House of Representatives holds provincial officials in contempt and orders them detained. The Court of Appeals grants a writ of habeas corpus and provisionally releases them. The House issues a show-cause order against the three CA Justices to explain why they should not be cited in contempt. May the House cite the Justices in contempt? Explain.
TW.q: May the House cite the CA Justices in contempt? Explain.
TW.hint: Who disciplines judges? What is Congress's contempt power for?
alac: No. The House may not cite the Justices in contempt.

The Constitution gives the Supreme Court administrative supervision over all courts and their personnel, and judges can be disciplined only by the Supreme Court. Congress's contempt power is incidental to its inquiry in aid of legislation. [Beyond the 28 cases: verify against your notes.]

Here, the Justices were deciding a habeas corpus petition, which is a judicial act. They are not witnesses in a legislative inquiry. Punishing them for a ruling would interfere with judicial independence and the separation of powers.
Therefore, the House cannot cite the Justices in contempt.
TW.key: TWIST: Castañeda shows that the Supreme Court controls discipline of judges. Congress cannot punish a court for how it rules.

TW.label: Someone else took the bar exam
TW.facts: A lawyer's admission is challenged after it is shown that another person took the bar exam for him. He has practiced honestly for ten years. Should he be removed? Explain.
TW.hint: Can honest years cure fraud?
alac: Yes. He should be removed.
Jurisprudence provides that the practice of law is a privilege, and admission obtained by fraud is void. Years of honest practice do not cure it.
Here, the exam was taken by another person, so the admission was fraudulent.
Therefore, his admission is void.
TW.key: Fraud at admission cannot be cured.

TW.label: Hidden criminal conviction
TW.facts: An applicant for the bar hid a conviction for a crime involving moral turpitude and was admitted. The conviction is discovered later. Should he be removed? Explain.
TW.hint: Is moral fitness needed at admission?
alac: Yes. He should be removed.
Jurisprudence provides that moral fitness must exist at admission and continue. Admission obtained by concealment is void.
Here, he concealed a conviction showing a lack of moral fitness.
Therefore, his admission is void.
TW.key: Concealing facts about moral fitness is fraud on admission.

TW.label: Honest clerical error
TW.facts: A lawyer's records show a wrong school year because of a clerical error by the registrar. He has all the required education and honestly passed the exam. A complainant asks to void his admission. Should the Court do so? Explain.
TW.q: Should the Court void his admission? Explain.
TW.hint: Was there fraud?
alac: No. The Court should not void his admission.
Jurisprudence provides that admission to the Bar obtained by fraud is void. Here, there was no fraud, and the lawyer has the education and passed the exam.
The error was the registrar's, and it did not affect his qualifications.
Therefore, his admission stands.
TW.key: TWIST: the rule is about fraud. An honest error that does not change qualifications is not fraud.

TW.label: Acting COA Chair
TW.facts: The COA Chair dies in office. The President issues an order designating the senior Commissioner as acting Chair until a new one is appointed. A taxpayer questions the order. Is it valid? Explain.
TW.hint: Who may choose the acting head: the President or the Commission?
alac: No. The designation is invalid.

Jurisprudence provides that the President cannot designate an acting head of a Constitutional Commission, even temporarily, because a designation revocable by the President makes the officer dependent on the President.
Here, the President chose the acting Chair. This is the dependence that Brillantes bars.
Therefore, the Commission should decide who acts.
TW.key: The Commission decides who acts as its head.

TW.label: Undersecretary as COMELEC OIC
TW.facts: The COMELEC Chairman is on long leave. The President names an undersecretary of a department as officer-in-charge of the Commission. A candidate questions the move. Is it valid? Explain.
TW.hint: Can an official from outside, picked by the President, run the Commission?
alac: No. The designation is invalid.
Jurisprudence provides that the President cannot designate an acting chairman of a Constitutional Commission. An undersecretary is an alter ego of the President.
Here, the OIC comes from the Executive and was chosen by the President, which is worse than a mere acting chair.
Therefore, the designation is invalid.
TW.key: The President cannot place executive officials at the head of a Constitutional Commission.

TW.label: Commission picks its own acting head
TW.facts: The COA Chair is abroad for a month. The members of the Commission meet and choose the senior Commissioner to be acting Chair. The President objects. Is the choice valid? Explain.
TW.hint: Who may decide a temporary arrangement under Brillantes?
alac: Yes. The choice is valid.
Jurisprudence provides that a temporary arrangement is for the Commission itself to decide.
Here, the Commission itself chose.
Therefore, the President's objection fails.
TW.key: TWIST: the problem in Brillantes is the President's designation, not temporary leadership itself.

TW.label: Commissioner made Chair after term expires
TW.facts: The term of the COA Chair expires on its seventh year. A sitting Commissioner, who has served three years, is appointed Chair. How long is the Chair's term? Explain.
TW.q: How long is the new Chair's term? Explain.
TW.hint: Did the predecessor's term expire or end early?
alac: The new Chair gets a full seven years as Chair, but total service as Commissioner and Chair may not go beyond seven years.
Jurisprudence provides that an expired term is followed by a full seven-year term. But total service can never be over seven years.

Here, the term expired, so the Chair starts a new seven-year term. Since the person already served three years as Commissioner, total service would be ten years, which the Constitution does not allow.
Therefore, the appointment is good for only four more years.
TW.key: Full term follows expiry, but total service is capped at seven.

TW.label: Successor given too long a term
TW.facts: A COA Chair resigns after two years. The President appoints a successor to a fresh seven-year term. The appointee insists on serving seven years. Is he correct? Explain.
TW.hint: Why did the vacancy arise?
alac: No. He is wrong.
Jurisprudence provides that when the vacancy arises from resignation, the appointee serves only the unexpired portion.
Here, the predecessor resigned after two years, so five years remain.
Therefore, the appointee serves five years only.
TW.key: Resignation → unexpired portion.

TW.label: Commissioner fills an unexpired term
TW.facts: A Commissioner who has served four years is appointed Chair to fill a vacancy that arose from the resignation of the former Chair, who has three years left. How long may the new Chair serve? Explain.
TW.q: How long may the new Chair serve? Explain.
TW.hint: Add the service in both posts and apply the cap.
alac: Three years as Chair, and in no case beyond a total of seven years.
Jurisprudence provides that an appointee to a vacancy serves only the unexpired portion, and total service is never over seven years.
Here, three years remain in the Chair's term, and the Commissioner already served four. Four plus three equals seven, which is the limit.
Therefore, the new Chair may serve three years.
TW.key: TWIST: add the years in both posts. Seven is the cap.

TW.label: Governor's private secretary
TW.facts: A governor appoints a private secretary who is removed when the governor's term ends. The secretary says the CSC classified the post as career service. Who is correct? Explain.
TW.hint: Apply the proximity rule.
alac: No. The secretary is wrong.
Jurisprudence provides that courts decide by the nature of the job whether it is primarily confidential, and the proximity rule looks at closeness to the appointing power.
Here, a private secretary works closely with the governor.
Therefore, the post is primarily confidential and the term ends with the governor's.
TW.key: Close to the appointing power = confidential.

TW.label: Water district GM after a CSC ruling
TW.facts: The CSC rules that a water district GM is a career position. The board relies on the court's ruling that it is confidential. Whose ruling controls? Explain.
TW.hint: Who has the last word?
alac: The court's ruling controls.
Jurisprudence provides that courts, not the CSC, have the final say on whether a position is primarily confidential.
Here, the court classifies the post as confidential.
Therefore, the CSC's classification does not bind.
TW.key: Courts have the last word on classification.

TW.label: Driver labeled “confidential”
TW.facts: A mayor appoints a driver and labels the post “primarily confidential.” The mayor later ends the driver's term for loss of confidence. The driver sues. Who is correct? Explain.
TW.hint: Does the label control, or the actual functions?
alac: Yes. The driver is probably correct.
Jurisprudence provides that the nature of the job and its actual functions decide, not the label.
Here, a driver's actual functions are not of a close and trusting nature that need confidence.
Therefore, the position is not confidential and the driver was removed without cause.
TW.key: TWIST: the label means nothing. Function and proximity matter.

TW.label: Free space in magazines
TW.facts: COMELEC orders magazines to give candidates free pages. A magazine publisher objects. Is the order valid? Explain.
TW.hint: Is a magazine a print medium like a newspaper?
alac: No. The order is invalid.
Jurisprudence provides that forced donation of print space is a taking without just compensation, and not valid police power.
Here, magazines are print media with private space.
Therefore, the order is invalid.
TW.key: Print space is private property.

TW.label: Free banners on news websites
TW.facts: COMELEC orders news websites to carry free banner ads for candidates. A site owner objects. Is the order valid? Explain.
TW.hint: Is the space private property without a franchise?
alac: No. The order is invalid.
Jurisprudence provides that "supervise or regulate" does not include a power to take private property without pay.
Here, the website space is privately owned and the site has no franchise from the State.
Therefore, the order is invalid.
TW.key: No franchise, no free taking.

TW.label: Oplan Baklas
TW.facts: COMELEC issues a resolution limiting campaign posters outside common poster areas to 2 by 3 feet, and authorizing its officers to remove, confiscate, and destroy bigger ones, even on private property. A private school lets volunteers put up 10 by 15 foot tarpaulins for a mayoral candidate on its grounds. COMELEC officers forcibly enter the campus, remove the tarpaulins, and confiscate the murals. Will the school's petition prosper? Explain.
TW.q: Will the school's petition prosper? Explain.
TW.hint: Separate the size rule from the way it was enforced.
alac: In part. The size limit may be valid, but the forced entry, confiscation, and destruction are not.

Under the Constitution, COMELEC may supervise or regulate media during the election period, but jurisprudence provides that “supervise or regulate” does not include a power to take private property without just compensation. [Beyond the 28 cases: the free speech issue in size limits is also relevant; verify against your notes.] Due process also requires notice and hearing before property is destroyed.

Here, the tarpaulins are election propaganda for a single candidate, so the size limit may be a reasonable regulation. But the officers forcibly entered the school, took the murals, and destroyed them without notice or hearing. This is a taking of private property without due process.
Therefore, the petition prospers as to the confiscation and destruction. COMELEC may require compliance with the size limits through lawful means.
TW.key: TWIST: regulating is not taking. Even a valid rule needs a lawful way of enforcing it.

TW.label: Facebook ads before the campaign
TW.facts: A mayor files a COC and, before the campaign period starts, posts paid Facebook ads asking to be voted for. A rival asks for her disqualification. Will it succeed? Explain.
TW.hint: When does a person become a candidate for campaign offenses?
alac: No. It will not succeed.
Jurisprudence provides that a person who files a COC becomes a candidate only at the start of the campaign period.
Here, the ads were posted before then.
Therefore, no premature campaigning.
TW.key: No campaign offense before the campaign period.

TW.label: Rice bags with the mayor's name
TW.facts: Before the campaign period, a candidate who filed a COC distributes rice bags with his name on them. A rival asks to disqualify him for premature campaigning. Will it succeed? Explain.
TW.hint: Is the candidate yet a “candidate”?
alac: No. It will not succeed on the ground of premature campaigning.
Jurisprudence provides that the unlawful acts applicable to candidates take effect only at the start of the campaign period.
Here, the rice bags were handed out before it started.
Therefore, no premature campaigning.
TW.key: Same rule, different facts.

TW.label: Rally on the eve of the election
TW.facts: On the day before the election, a candidate holds a rally, though campaigning is forbidden that day. The candidate says Peñera allows such acts. Is the candidate correct? Explain.
TW.hint: Peñera is about acts before the campaign. What about after?
alac: No. The candidate is wrong.
Jurisprudence provides that acts done before the campaign period starts are not premature campaigning. It does not allow campaigning on days when it is forbidden after the period.
Here, the rally falls on a prohibited day, when the candidate is already a candidate.
Therefore, the rally may be penalized.
TW.key: TWIST: Peñera covers the period before the start, not after the campaign period ends.

TW.label: District representative's residency
TW.facts: A district representative has been proclaimed, has taken his oath, and has sat in the House. A voter files in COMELEC a petition to cancel his COC for lack of residency. Does COMELEC have jurisdiction? Explain.
TW.hint: Who decides after proclamation, oath, and assumption?
alac: No. The HRET does.
Jurisprudence provides that once proclaimed, sworn in, and in office, challenges belong to the HRET.
Here, all three are done.
Therefore, the petition belongs in the HRET.
TW.key: Proclaimed + oath + seated = HRET.

TW.label: Senator-elect's citizenship
TW.facts: A senator was proclaimed, took oath, and assumed office. A petition on his citizenship is filed in COMELEC. Where should it be filed? Explain.
TW.q: Where should the petition be filed? Explain.
TW.hint: What body hears Senate election contests?
alac: In the Senate Electoral Tribunal.

Jurisprudence provides that once a member has been proclaimed, sworn in and assumed office, only the electoral tribunal can hear the challenge. [For the Senate, the tribunal is the SET, by Under the Constitution, .]
Here, the senator already assumed office.
Therefore, COMELEC has no jurisdiction.
TW.key: The House has the HRET and the Senate the SET.

TW.label: Proclaimed but not yet assumed
TW.facts: A nominee has been proclaimed but has not yet taken the oath or assumed office. A petition is filed in COMELEC against him. Does COMELEC have jurisdiction? Explain.
TW.hint: Which of the three steps is missing?
alac: Yes. COMELEC still has jurisdiction.
Jurisprudence provides that the HRET gains jurisdiction only after the nominee has been proclaimed, sworn in, and has assumed office.
Here, only proclamation is done.
Therefore, COMELEC may still act.
TW.key: TWIST: all three steps are needed before HRET takes over.

TW.label: Late party registration
TW.facts: A new party files for registration after the deadline. COMELEC grants it, saying it wants to widen participation. A rival questions. Is the grant valid? Explain.
TW.hint: Are the deadlines mandatory?
alac: No. The grant is invalid.
Jurisprudence provides that registration deadlines are mandatory, and granting late registration is grave abuse of discretion.
Here, COMELEC granted a late application.
Therefore, the grant is invalid.
TW.key: Deadlines are mandatory.

TW.label: Unregistered coalition seeks accreditation
TW.facts: A coalition of parties that never registered asks to be accredited. COMELEC says registration is unnecessary because the parties are already registered. Is COMELEC correct? Explain.
TW.hint: Does the coalition have to register itself?
alac: No. COMELEC is wrong.
Jurisprudence provides that a coalition must register before it can be accredited.
Here, the coalition never registered.
Therefore, accreditation should be denied.
TW.key: Coalition must register itself before accreditation.

TW.label: Coalition registered on time
TW.facts: A coalition registers on time, and COMELEC accredits it. A rival says COMELEC had no discretion since registration just recognizes a fact. Is the rival correct? Explain.
TW.hint: What kind of act is registration?
alac: No. The rival is wrong.
Jurisprudence provides that registration is not mere recognition of an operative fact. It requires discretion and quasi-judicial evaluation.
Here, the coalition registered on time and COMELEC evaluated it.
Therefore, the accreditation is valid.
TW.key: TWIST: on-time registration with evaluation is fine.

TW.label: COA clerk files certiorari
TW.facts: A COA clerk is dismissed for dishonesty and files a petition for certiorari in the Supreme Court. Is this the proper remedy? Explain.
TW.q: Is this the proper remedy? Explain.
TW.hint: Where does a COA employee appeal?
alac: No. The proper remedy is an appeal to the CSC.
Jurisprudence provides that when COA disciplines its own staff, the remedy is appeal to the CSC.
Here, the clerk went to the Supreme Court.
Therefore, the petition is dismissed.
TW.key: COA employees → CSC.

TW.label: Auditor paid as consultant
TW.facts: A COA auditor is hired as a paid consultant by an agency he audits. He says that no law bars this. Is he correct? Explain.
TW.hint: Can an auditor take benefits from the audited?
alac: No. He is wrong.
Jurisprudence provides that auditors may not take benefits from the agencies they audit.
Here, he was paid by the agency he audits.
Therefore, he is liable administratively.
TW.key: Auditors may not accept anything from audited agencies.

TW.label: Arthur's old laptop
TW.facts: Arthur, a staff of the Office of the President's public assistance office, is told to hand over his office-issued laptop for a replacement. The technical team finds a folder with back-up data from his personal phone, showing that he solicited and accepted bribes in exchange for expediting assistance requests. Charged administratively, Arthur says his privacy was violated because the data came from his personal device, and that the evidence is inadmissible. Is Arthur correct? Explain.
TW.hint: Whose device was searched, and what standard of evidence applies in administrative cases?
alac: No. Arthur is not correct.

The right to privacy depends on a reasonable expectation of privacy. [Beyond the 28 cases: this follows the ruling on searches of government workplaces; verify against your notes.] Jurisprudence provides that substantial evidence is enough in administrative cases. Public officers must also act with integrity, and taking benefits in exchange for official acts is serious misconduct.

Here, the laptop was office-issued, given for official work, and being returned to the employer. The technical team was scanning it as part of a routine replacement, not as a hunt for evidence. Arthur chose to store backup of his personal phone on an office device, which lowers any expectation of privacy. The messages, which show bribe solicitation, are relevant and likely meet the standard of substantial evidence.
Therefore, the evidence is admissible, and Arthur may be charged administratively.
TW.key: TWIST: the standard is substantial evidence, and a routine scan of an office laptop gives little room for privacy. [Pollo is outside the 28 cases.]

TW.label: GOCC governance fee
TW.facts: The Governance Commission for GOCCs demands that BSP pay a governance fee under the GOCC law. BSP refuses. Who is correct? Explain.
TW.hint: Is the BSP a GOCC?
alac: BSP is correct.
Jurisprudence provides that the BSP is not a GOCC because it has no stock and no members.
Here, GOCC laws don't apply to it.
Therefore, the fee is not due.
TW.key: Not a GOCC → no GOCC fee.

TW.label: BSP refuses COA audit
TW.facts: The BSP refuses any COA audit, saying it is not a GOCC. Is the refusal valid? Explain.
TW.hint: Does being a non-GOCC stop an audit?
alac: No. The refusal is invalid.
Jurisprudence provides that the BSP is not a GOCC, but COA still audits it.
Here, the BSP is a government instrumentality.
Therefore, COA may audit.
TW.key: Not a GOCC ≠ no audit.

TW.label: Government-owned stock bank
TW.facts: A government bank has stock owned by the Republic and is created by a charter. It argues that BSP v. COA shows that it is not a GOCC either. Is the bank correct? Explain.
TW.hint: Why was BSP not a GOCC?
alac: No. The bank is wrong.
Jurisprudence provides that BSP was not a GOCC because it has no stock and no members.
Here, the bank has stock owned by the government.
Therefore, it is a GOCC.
TW.key: TWIST: stock is the difference.

TW.label: Seaport authority's piers
TW.facts: A city taxes the piers owned by a port authority created by law. The authority says the piers are public dominion. Who is correct? Explain.
TW.hint: Is the property of public dominion?
alac: The authority is correct.
Jurisprudence provides that property of public dominion owned by the Republic is exempt from real property tax.
Here, the piers are for public use.
Therefore, the tax is invalid.
TW.key: Public dominion = exempt.

TW.label: Runway put up for auction
TW.facts: A city auctions a runway for unpaid real property tax. Is the auction valid? Explain.
TW.hint: Can public dominion property be sold for tax?
alac: No. The auction is invalid.
Jurisprudence provides that airport lands and buildings are of public dominion and can't be sold at auction for taxes.
Here, the runway is such property.
Therefore, the auction is void.
TW.key: No tax auction of public dominion property.

TW.label: Government-owned hotel corporation
TW.facts: A city taxes a hotel owned by a government corporation with stock. The corporation cites MIAA. Is the corporation exempt? Explain.
TW.hint: Is it an instrumentality or a corporation?
alac: No. It is not exempt.
Jurisprudence provides that a government instrumentality holding property of public dominion is exempt from real property tax. A GOCC with stock is taxable.
Here, the hotel is commercial property, not public dominion.
Therefore, it is taxable.
TW.key: TWIST: MIAA protects instrumentalities and public dominion, not commercial GOCC property.

TW.label: CHR creates new positions
TW.facts: The CHR creates 50 new positions without DBM approval. DBM refuses to fund them. Who is correct? Explain.
TW.hint: Is the CHR fiscally autonomous?
alac: DBM is correct.
Jurisprudence provides that the CHR doesn't have fiscal autonomy and so needs DBM approval.
Here, no approval was given.
Therefore, the positions are not funded.
TW.key: No fiscal autonomy → DBM approval.

TW.label: Agency called “independent” by its charter
TW.facts: A law calls a new agency "independent and fiscally autonomous." The agency invokes this against DBM. Is it correct? Explain.
TW.hint: Who has fiscal autonomy: only those in the Constitution?
alac: No. The agency is wrong.
Jurisprudence provides that only the J-C-O (Judiciary, Constitutional Commissions, Ombudsman) have fiscal autonomy.
Here, the agency is not among them, whatever the law calls it.
Therefore, the agency needs DBM approval.
TW.key: Only J-C-O.

TW.label: COMELEC uses its savings
TW.facts: COMELEC uses its savings to upgrade positions without DBM approval. DBM objects. Who is correct? Explain.
TW.hint: Is COMELEC in the J-C-O?
alac: COMELEC is correct.
Jurisprudence provides that the Constitutional Commissions have fiscal autonomy.
Here, COMELEC is a Constitutional Commission.
Therefore, it may use its savings.
TW.key: TWIST: unlike CHR, COMELEC is a J-C-O member.
